[Figure: Sepia photograph of Arthur Schopenhauer resting his head on his hand]

Schopenhauer, Arthur

1788 1860 CE
Pessimism, Ethics

Arthur was an atheist, German philosopher who came from a very wealthy family. This allowed him to enjoy life as a young man. In his younger days, he picked up chorus girls from stage doors on a regular basis. It's doubtful that this was for the purpose of discussing philosophy with them. His family relations and lack of friends probably had some influence on his psyche and gloomy philosophy. Arthur's father committed suicide when Schopenhauer was 17. After this, Arthur's mother enjoyed life as a youngish widower, taking a number of lovers. She was smart and a successful novelist who was, for a time, a leading figure in German social and literary circles, for a time. Goethe was a friend.

Arthur disapproved greatly of his mother's behaviour. He failed to see that his own behaviour was not very different. He also appeared to be jealous of her position as a clever, independent woman. Arthur wanted to be regarded as the figure of importance and the sole genius in his family.

Perhaps not surprisingly his philosophy was pessimistic, basically claiming that everything is hopeless. Unlike Plato, Kant and others who thought there was some room for reason in the world Arthur saw the world as irrational and unable to escape from evil. People are full of unsatisfied desires, according to him. The only thing to be done, he said, was to renounce desire. Something after Gautama here and his four noble truths. Gautama, or Buddha, was his

predecessor by 1700 years. In fact, Arthur had a four of his own. He identified four different categories each of which had its own associated reasoning:

(1) Material things; associated reasoning is cause and effect;
(2) Abstract concepts; reasoning here is in terms of logic;
(3) Mathematical and Geometrical constructions; reasoning in respect of numbers and space;
(4) Psychologically motivating forces; where moral reasoning or intention must be used.

This position of hopelessness, he thought, was slightly redeemed by the arts and philosophy. He said: "Creatures of will, we cannot stop striving. In art, we retreat from light." His main theory was centred on the will, and set out in his work "The World as Will and Idea" in 1818. Here he said the will was the main, sometimes bad, influence on human character, consciousness and intellect. Conflict between opposing wills caused endless dispute and frustration. In his ethical philosophy, he introduced the moral will. he said we should take an empathic position with others, through our moral will.

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Ralph Waldo Emerson]

Emerson, Ralph Waldo

1803 to 1882 CE
Transcendentalism, Pantheism, Ethics

Here is an American who in the philosophical pantheon was known as a leading figure of the New England Transcendentalists. Ralph was mainly a writer of essays, sermons and poems. He emphasised the importance of personal integrity and morals and believed in the unity of all nature, a sort of pantheism. For Ralph, this meant that everything, mind and matter, was a part of a continuing whole, including the divine being. He thought people should be self-reliant and were capable of reaching any goal (very American). He said: "a man in debt is so far a slave". This is not quite so in keeping with modern America where household debt usually exceeds $10 trillion. Ralph also stresses that we should live in harmony with nature (again not commonly so much the America of today). Be daring and explore outside of your comfort zone was his view: "Do not go where the path may lead, go instead where there is no path and leave a trail.", and "All life is an experiment. The more experiments you make the better." He also stressed the importance of keeping good relations with other people: "You cannot do a kindness too soon, for you never know how soon it will be too late." and "The only way to have a friend is to be one."

Ralph was a founder of transcendentalism. This was a move away from what he saw as the stultifying reliance on the Scriptures for intellectual guidance in the eastern USA.

His transcendentalist approach claimed that current religious and political institutions were corrupting of individuals. People were at their best, he thought, when self-reliant and independent. They had inherent goodness which could create a true community. He influenced Nietzsche to some extent (although the latter did not believe in a divine being).

[Figure: Black and white photograph of John Stuart Mill]

Mill, John Stuart

1806 to 1873 CE
Empiricism,
Utilitarianism, Liberalism

Mill was probably the greatest English philosopher of his century. On his death, an admiring fellow philosopher Henry Sidgwick said:" 'I should say that from about 1860-65, or thereabouts, he ruled England in the region of thought as very few men ever did." Mill was extremely precocious as a child, reading Plato, Xenophon and others in Greek by the age of eight. He was encouraged to constantly study by his father and was denied a normal childhood. All this caused him to have a nervous breakdown at the age of 21. Later, he had a happier personal life in marriage to Harriet whom he idolised and thought was his intellectual equal. She was a strong advocate of women's rights, as was Mill.

Mill was a utilitarian, his interest sparked by his father's friend, the philosopher Jeremy Bentham. But he realised some of the potential problems with Bentham's straightforward, utilitarianism. For instance, applying Bentham's idea you could have a situation incompatible with generally accepted moral standards. Three torturers could get more pleasure from their action than their single victim would experience (unless he/she was an extreme masochist!) Strict application of Bentham would say this was a good, utilitarian outcome – the most pleasure for most people. To counter this sort of utilitarian problem Mill added another element that must be considered. In addition to Bentham's quantity of pleasure Mill said the <u>quality</u> of pleasure must also be a relevant factor.

As a result, Bentham philosophy has been defined as <u>act</u> utilitarianism and Mill as <u>rule</u> utilitarianism. He also said the pleasures gained from a deep-thinking mind were superior to those of the flesh.

John Stuart, a question for you, how much does the mind have to be engaged in order to trump all fleshly pleasures? Why can't we have both at once, e.g. eating a sumptuous meal while thinking about the nature of reality!

Mill did not just dwell on the theoretical aspects of utilitarianism He proposed many liberal and practical sociological actions in written works, his greatest being "On Liberty". Here are some:

give women the right to vote;
reform labour unions and co-operatives;
reform Parliament by introducing proportional representation and the single transferrable vote.;
reform divorce laws to give women equal rights;
allow women to become jurors.

He backed up these ideas with forceful argument in Parliament where he was an MP. In economics, he was a free marketeer and did not believe in progressive taxation, with a bigger tax rate for high-income earners. Mill believed this punished the hard working, successful people and rewarded those who could try harder, but he did favour inheritance tax. He was not a believer in religion. He was an atheist. Some of the many notable things he said, along the lines of Epicurus: "Pleasure and freedom from pain, are the only things desirable as ends." He also anticipated some aspects of the 1948 United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights saying: "The only freedom which deserves the name is that of pursuing our own good, in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it." Mill gave some empirical advice too: "There are many truths of which the full meaning cannot be realized until personal experience has brought it home." What a great liberal he was.

[Figure: Pencil drawing portrait of Kierkegaard]

Kierkegaard, Soren

1813 to 1855 CE
Existentialism

Here is a dogged, great Dane who said mankind's greatest gift was freewill. He was a theologian as well as a philosopher, although the distinction between the two can be a fine line.

Kierkegaard is best known as the father of existentialism, although he did not know this because the term was invented late in the 19th century.

His existentialist position stemmed from a view that it was the individual person who gave meaning to life. He excluded society generally and religion.

Soren was a tortured figure. His father was a gloomy, deeply religious man who imposed strict rules of behaviour on his family. This had a lifetime effect on Kierkegaard who said that he did not have a childhood and was born old. This may explain why he wrote on many darker philosophical and psychological topics such as: anxiety, despair, melancholy, inwardness, irony, inherited sin, love as a duty, and sacrifice. He used Socratic techniques through irony to attack conventional forms of knowledge and forced people to think for themselves, like Socrates.

Soren was a trenchant critic of Hegel. Hegel thought it possible to make all knowledge known through his dialectical, logic method. Kierkegaard had a different approach. He sought to take away knowledge leaving knowledge ultimately solely to God. Some of the things he said: "Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards."; "The highest and most beautiful things in life are not to be heard about, nor read about, nor seen but, if one will, are to be lived." and "If I am capable of grasping God objectively, I do not believe, but precisely because I cannot do this I must believe." and "God does not think, he creates. He does not exist; he is eternal." For Soren God is always here and God's here is always now.

On the subject of the Bible and difficulty of its interpretation he said: "The Bible is very easy to understand. But we Christians are a bunch of scheming swindlers. We pretend to be unable to understand it because we know very well that the minute we understand, we are obliged to act accordingly." Really Soren? You seem to suggest that understanding must inevitably be followed by belief and action.

[Figure: Painted portrait of Karl Marx holding up two fingers in a V sign]

Marx, Karl

1818 to 1883 CE
Political

Not many philosophers before or after Marx can say they underpinned a revolution, perhaps only Locke and Paine, maybe Rousseau, but Marx, a German political philosopher, is without doubt one who can make this claim; not once but at least thrice.

His major works: "The Communist Manifesto" (1848) and "Das Kapital" (1867–1894) were the basis for the Russian (later expanded to the Soviet

Union) and Chinese communist (the People's Republic of China) revolutions, then we must not forget Cuba, despite this was a much smaller affair.

Marx said states, i.e. countries, were run by the ruling classes for their own benefit. He saw this as unfair. This led him to promote socialism because it would support the common interest of all rather than the few. His thoughts can be argued as having some similarity with Bentham's utilitarianism, in that they stress the importance of the whole of society rather than the individual: "Society does not consist of individuals but expresses the sum of interrelations, the relations within which these individuals stand." He threatened the ruling classes with revolution: "Let the ruling classes tremble at a communist revolution. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. Working men of all countries, unite!" and, slightly curiously but no doubt partially approved by Mary Wollstonecraft: "Anyone who knows anything of history knows that great social changes are impossible without feminine upheaval. Social progress can be measured exactly by the social position of the fair sex, the ugly ones included." Mary would take Karl to task over those last few words though. Time has revealed the problem with Karl's communism. Those countries that have apparently embraced it still end up with a very privileged few at the top of the tree.

[Figure: Oval portrait photograph of Charles Sanders Peirce]

Peirce, Charles Sanders

1839 to 1914 CE
Pragmatism

Charles was an American philosopher. Not only that he also managed to be a logician, mathematician, and scientist. His main claim to philosophical fame is as the originator of pragmatism. He might have been even more famously known as the inventor of computers. He had the idea that in switching electrical circuits these could be used in making logical operations. Sadly, he did not develop this correct theory. It was decades later that computers were invented.

His pragmatic views are the sort that often give philosophers a bad name with the general population. The pragmatism promoted by Peirce says that thoughts main function is to decide action, make predictions or solve problems. It was not to hold a mirror up to reality. To most people this may seem stating the "bleeding obvious".

Peirce' views were partially founded on his scientific mind. He held some support for both Kant and Hegel but clearly had a jaundiced view of some philosophers: "It will sometimes strike a scientific man that the philosophers

have been less intent on finding out what the facts are, than on inquiring what belief is most in harmony with their system." And he explains why there are so many religions and why people hold beliefs: "Doubt is an uneasy and dissatisfied state from which we struggle to free ourselves and pass into the state of belief; while the latter is a calm and satisfactory state which we do not wish to avoid, or to change to a belief in anything else."

Of himself he said: "There is a kink in my damned brain that prevents me from thinking as other people think." It's good that you had that kink Charles.

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Friedrich Nietzsche]

Nietzsche, Frederick

1844 to 1900 CE
Existentialism, Nihilism

Fred (I will call him this, it's easier to pronounce and write than his surname.) Fred was a German philosopher, poet and composer. Descartes apart, Fred made the most well-known statement in philosophy: "God is dead". This comment is quite well known.

Fred's concerns with God partly stems from the time he lived in. He read Darwin and understood that evolution was contingent (i.e. by chance) rather than, as had been widely promoted by many religions and beliefs, by telos (purpose). This affected Fred's views on nihilism (life has no meaning or purpose). Before Darwin, an Abrahamic God was firmly in place for many. This belief in God was a huge counter to the apparent hopelessness of nihilism. With God, we have intrinsic values, a basis for knowledge and a justification for evil in the world. In this sense Christianity gave comfort in promoting a certainty and was a great buffer to the gloomy despair fostered by nihilism. Fred thought nihilism needed to be accepted but it should be fought against. Did Fred's despairing nihilist views arise because he was severely affected by a combination of: poor medical health, (particularly mental health); acceptance of proof that God did not exist; and his forceful sister's hard racial views? Fred's possible answer to how nihilism could be defeated was by the emergence of a Superman, Ubermench.  This new, superior being would supplant existing humanity and its crumbling values. Had Fred lived in modern times he might have taken comfort from the possibility that scientific rationalisation gives defeat to nihilism.

In his book "Beyond Good and Evil" he criticised past philosophers for their acceptance of moral precepts and, with further originality, said that sometimes 'lies' could be preferable to 'truth'. These thoughts contributed to his concern with nihilism.

Fred had interesting views in several other areas. He thought the individual made free choices over values and beliefs and through this determined what sort of person emerges. He pontificated on both marriage and art: "When marrying, ask yourself this question: Do you believe that you will be able to converse well with this person into your old age? Everything else in marriage is transitory."

And, "Without music, life would be a mistake." Poor Fred suffered mood swings and bouts of depression. At the age of 44 he went into an asylum for a while. He also suffered physically and died comparatively young (at age 56), probably from brain cancer.

Not only were his mental and physical health the subject of doctoring, he also had his ideas doctored, by his sister, Elizabeth.

She was anti-Semitic and an ardent nationalist. [Figure: Black and white photograph of Gottlob Frege]

Frege, Gottlob

1848 to 1925 CE
Analytic, Logic

This Professor of Mathematics was yet another in the line-up of noted German philosophers. Gottlob was around at the same time as fellow Germans, Marx, Nietzsche and Heidegger. He also followed not far behind Hegel and Schopenhauer. Gottlob had an interest in the logic of arithmetic and in language. In logical musings, he followed on from Aristotle who was perhaps the originator of the use of logic in philosophy. Maybe Gottlob was also inspired to think outside the box because he doubted the seeming certainty claimed by his contemporaries.

He thought there had to be a surer, analytical way at arriving at knowledge and true understanding than the opinionated utterances of fellow German practitioners and others. So, he developed an analytic, logic-based system. Gottlob led quite a secluded life with no particular major events to disturb his peace. This environment probably gave him the time to think deep, original thoughts.

He brought about a sea-change in Western philosophical thinking by giving up on traditional deductive logic and originating a new symbolic, formal version. In 1884 his "The Foundations of Arithmetic" appeared in print.

He explained his new logic where he thought he was able to make firm connections between mathematics and logic. He demonstrated that numbers are not objects, like cows or doors. He said: "Numbers are the properties of concepts or useful logical fictions - rather like the fiction of the average man." This led the way for those 20th century philosophers who took up the analytic method. Gottlob did not stop with maths and logic. He also had a look at language where he thought meaning attributed through language, was not just about the what of an object but also its sense. Here he said that the sense of a language depended on its conventional, public use and this can change. A simple example is the use of the word "gay". Before the 1970's reference to a gay person would be interpreted as meaning that person was jolly. In more modern parlance the term refers to a homosexual person. Bertrand Russell took up and developed some of Gottlob's ideas. He both impressed and influenced Wittgenstein. The latter was encouraged to go to Cambridge to study with Russell.

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Edmund Husserl]

Husserl, Edmund

1859 to 1938 CE
Phenomenology

He was born in part of the then Austrian Empire, now the Czech Republic. Husserl was another philosopher who was an originator and father. His child is phenomenology. This is a topic very much in vogue with 20th century philosophers. Phenomenology is about consciousness and its analysis. Husserl said that our consciousness is always directed to an object, basically anything that springs to mind: a birthday cake; football match; or contemplating dawn. The object may be simple but the detail is complicated. Husserl said consciousness did not give or assume reality of an object, it merely suggested an "as if" it exists. Husserl took up the concept of intentionality, i.e. thought about something, from the work of Franz Brentano, a German priest and philosopher. It is much explored in modern philosophy of mind.

Interesting to apply the Husserl analysis to the ontological argument for a God. He expressed his ideas in three volumes called, strangely, "Ideas". Husserl did not fully complete his work and is generally reckoned to have a poor writing style. He is listed as a philosophical great because of his ideas on

phenomenology and its relevance today, especially in sociology and the philosophy of the mind. He said: "All philosophical disciplines are rooted in pure phenomenology, through whose development, and through it alone, they obtain their proper force. " and Husserl's famous principle of all principles: "that everything originally... offered to us in 'intuition' is to be accepted simply as what it is presented as being, but also only within the limits in which it is presented there." In essence Husserl thought we could only have perceptions of true reality; actual reality was beyond us.

Husserl when dying, refused spiritual guidance and comfort, saying he wished to die as a philosopher.

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Henri Bergson]

Bergson, Henri

1859 to 1941 CE
Time, mind

Here we have a Jewish, Frenchman who was the most famous philosopher in the early part of the twentieth century, and very popular. His lectures in Paris and New York were always crowded out.

'Time' is appropriate to mention. His unique thoughts about time were Henri's crowning achievement. He set out his ideas in: "Time and Freewill: An Essay on the Immediate Data of Consciousness (1889)."

Ideas about time in the 1880's fell into two categories: 1. The older version was known as Newtonian absolutism which said time is independent, it's always there, even if there is nothing else in the universe. 2. Kantian idealism of time, here Kant, although accepting the Newtonian version, thought time is intrinsic to our minds. We cannot perceive the world but in terms of time. These ideas captured Bergson's interest. He concluded that our spatial concept of time, where we divide it into seconds, minutes, hours, days and years, was not the full story. These 'times' were all based on special concepts, such as the time that the Earth took to go around the sun and time it took for the Earth revolved on its axis.

They did not represent the human experience. He wrote: "We give a mechanical explanation of a fact and then substitute the explanation for the fact itself." Lived time has 'real duration, (durée réelle)', according to Bergson, not like the artificial spacial measurement. Our experience of time is as if it were a flow where the past penetrates into the presence.

Some philosophers thought Bergson viewed time in an original way. William James was impressed, others not so. Bertrand Russell, was highly sceptical. He claimed Bergson was not logically rigorous enough. Bergson also upset Albert Einstein, whose showed the link between time and space in his theory of "General Relativity". In 1922 they had a public debate where Einstein was seen to be the winner on points, but at another time, who knows what the outcome, Einstein might become second.

After these deep timely thoughts, and his verbal and written expression of them, Gilbert did not stop thinking.

He must have had more time on his hands because of his new focus, the mind vis a vis the body. In 1896 out came: "Matter and Memory". This was in direct refutation of Theodule Ribot who purported that memory was lodged in a section of the brain. It was of a material nature. Bergson saw memory as a spiritual entity that assisted the brain in determining present action. For Bergson memory was entirely separate from the body. He was also critical of Descartes dualism. Bergson, said Rene defined mind and body as substance, whereas one, concerned with memory, was not. It was of a spiritual nature.

His last book, "The Creative Mind", introduces us to Bergson's foray into analytic method. He says: "What philosophy has lacked most of all is precision. Philosophical systems are not cut to the measure of the reality in which we live; they are too wide for reality." Here he is explaining his opposition to philosophical generalities. This is curious, given Russell's trenchant criticism of Bergson and what he saw as woolly thinking.

The Nobel Prize Committee did not agree with Bertrand. They gave the 1927 Literature Prize to Bergson saying: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1927 was awarded to Henri Bergson "in recognition of his rich and vitalizing ideas and the brilliant skill with which they have been presented." Who gets your vote, William James and the Nobel Committee, or Bertrand Russell?

Russell, Bertrand

1872 1970 CE
Epistemology

Bertrand was the son of Viscount and Viscountess Amberley, who were very radical for their time - supporting birth-control for one thing. They asked John Stuart Mill to be his godparent. Bertrand was certainly influenced by him, hence his leaning towards

utilitarianism. Bertrand probably lived longer than any other great philosopher. He died just 2 years short of a century. He could have kicked the bucket much earlier than 1970. In October 1948, en route to lecturing in Trondheim, Bertrand's airplane crashed in the sea. 19 of the 43 passengers drowned. One of the survivors was Bertrand. Paradoxically he claimed that he owed his life to smoking because the people who drowned were in the non-smoking part of the plane. Another unusual claim to fame is his appearance as the narrator in a graphic novel: "Logicomix: An Epic Search for Truth." Bertrand was born in Wales but lived much of his life at Pembroke Lodge, in Richmond Park, London. Here he could stroll around the trees surrounding his house. But Bertrand was more of a man who could see the woods rather than the trees. His analytical philosophy allowed him to see the bigger picture. For a philosopher, he had an unusual advantage in that he was easy to read. This skill probably helped win him the Nobel prize for literature in 1950 mainly for his "History of Philosophy" and "The Problems of Philosophy". It's a wonder he had time to do much writing, he was quite a lad with the ladies and married four times, but he knew many more women than just four.

He was not only a philosopher, he was also publicly active in promoting his libertarian views, speaking against war and nuclear weapons and campaigning for civil rights. He spent some time in prison as a result. In philosophy, he used a logical-analytical method to argue alongside philosopher G.E. Moore against the rise of British Idealism (an offshoot of Kant's world of appearances, stemming from the mind, and of Hegel's Absolute, this, a sort of cosmic super thing.) Along with A.N. Whitehead he wrote "Principia Mathematica". His efforts against Idealism killed it off. Logical analysis, as expressed by Bertrand won the day.

Russell invented a term: sense-data, by this he meant that our senses give us one interpretation of what might be a different reality. Looking at a chair one sees a different view from the side than overhead.

Russell would say what is the real chair, we only experience that what are senses tell us. Russell thought we should tackle philosophical issues from a logical, mathematical basis.

Wittgenstein, Ludwig Josef Johann

1889 to 1951 CE
Language

Wittgenstein, born to a very wealthy Austrian was perhaps the leading philosopher of the 20th century. Some think he was the most important since Immanuel Kant. In his childhood, although it's hard to believe, he was in the same Primary School as a certain Adolf Hitler. They might have been in the same class although this is less likely. They were a class year apart. In the First World War Ludwig was in the Austrian army, which he felt to be his duty. Later in life he lived at first in Manchester, where he was interested in aeronautics and building and flying kites. After this he resided in unusual austerity at Trinity College, Cambridge having given away his inherited wealth. Here he became well acquainted with Bertrand Russell and from this contact developed an interest in philosophy.

His room at Trinity College, Cambridge consisted of a deckchair and a heater. He lived with a young male lover, Francis Skinner, who died of polio at age 29, Wittgenstein was devastated by his death.

Apart from his philosophical prominence he is also to the forefront in instrumental argumentation. He apparently waved a poker at Karl Popper. The two were having an argument at a meeting of the Moral Sciences Club in Cambridge. The dispute became heated, so the poker was very relevant!

[Figure: Black and white school photograph with arrows labelled "Ludwig Wittgenstein" and "Adolf Hitler". Caption: 1904 at the Realschule School, Linz, Austria. Wittgenstein (bottom left), Hitler (top, right) Is this right, were they really classmates? (use Ludwig's ordinary language philosophy to discuss "right". For starters, Hitler is certainly to the right of LW, both positionally and politically but is this the right right!)]

One curious possibility is that he knew Hitler as a child.

In his philosophy Wittgenstein started by finishing, and later changed his mind a bit and finished a second time. He was a soldier on the wrong side in WW1 and spent time in a prisoner of war camp.

He used this time productively to finish "Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus", which described the logical relationship between proposed ideas and the world. In "Tractatus" he described what he thought was the core of all philosophical problems. They were, he said, based on misunderstandings of the logic of language. Through this work he thought he had solved all philosophical problems in existence. So he brought philosophy to an end, you might think. But perhaps not, later he recanted on some of this in his "Philosophical Investigations." Here he outlined his philosophy of ordinary language, (OL) but still pursuing his "Tractatus" theme although in a less technical way.

OL philosophy is exactly what it says on the tin. It argues that for centuries philosophers have tried to give a meaning to words they use which is not the same meaning as ordinary usage of that word. Wikipedia gives this example associated with the meaning of reality: "What is reality? Philosophers have treated it as a noun denoting something that has certain properties. For thousands of years, they have debated those properties. Ordinary language philosophy instead looks at how we use the word reality in everyday language. In some instances, people will say, "It may seem that X is the case, but in reality, Y is the case"

Another example is given by Wittgenstein where he uses music to explain: "Understanding a sentence, in Philosophical Investigations, is more akin to understanding a theme in music than one may think."

What he is getting at is that our understanding, which must of necessity use language, is based on all the cultural and other baggage attached to words. We see a picture based on words, not just the word itself.

It certainly would have been helpful to general understanding if past philosophers had paid attention to Wittgenstein's ideas, particularly people who can be hard to follow like Kant, Hegel, Husserl and Heidegger.

Ludwig was a follower of Schopenhauer and claimed to have improved on the latter's philosophy. He thought that we should only discuss the phenomenal world, i.e. the world we live in and experience. For Wittgenstein, discussion of any other possible reality was out of bounds and we should keep silent about it. Wittgenstein, apart from altering his philosophical ideas slightly also changed his mind on religion. He was religious but at one stage confessed to his sisters that he had lost his faith. He found it again, probably not hard in the Spartan surrounding of his accommodation.

Humour had importance he claimed: "A serious and good philosophical work could be written consisting entirely of jokes." and "Never stay up on the barren heights of cleverness, but come down into the green valleys of silliness."

Ludwig's work on language is still relevant today. He pointed the way for the study of the mind and cognitive science which is firmly connected to the complexity of language. He said: "Language is a part of our organism and no less complicated than it." [Figure: Black and white photograph of Martin Heidegger]

Heidegger, Martin

1889 to 1976 CE
Metaphysics, Phenomenology, Naziism

What's unusual about Martin Heidegger in the philosopher's pantheon? Well, for one he was a signed-up Nazi with an admiration for Hitler, for another, not surprisingly, he was an anti-Semite.

He's not so much the black sheep among philosophers; more of a black shirt. Karl Popper though thought he was both. Hannah Arendt, his one-time girlfriend, seemingly ignored his darker side. But as a philosopher Heidegger, for all his sins, is counted as one of the greats of the 20th century.

His main work was: "Being and Time". He explored an ontological interest asking: "Why are there beings at all instead of nothing? That is the question." The base approach he used was the analysis of human existence, he called it "Dasein". MH was very dismissive of the technological leanings of his time which he saw as the road to nihilism. He went back to the pre-Socratics who were interested in fundamental reality. He also studied Kant, Hegel and Husserl. He offered a different slant on the latter's phenomenology viewpoint. Where Husserl thought that the conscious experience had prime importance, rather than the real object of that experience. For Heiddeger, consciousness is always because we are conscious, or aware of something, so it has an objective intention. We intend to have some thought about this object, which is not necessarily certain to be real. The intention itself arises through our involvement in the world so said Heidegger.

Thinking outside the box, he explored other areas too: poetry, architecture and technology. Interestingly, like his contemporary Wittgenstein he saw the importance of language. This he thought was the route to uncovering the question of being. This sounds most obvious but Heidegger had a more complex understanding of the use of language: "Man acts as though he were the shaper and master of language, while in fact language remains the master of man".

His concern with nihilism and the important counter provided by religious belief, whether or not true is shown in: "If God as the supra-sensory ground and goal of all reality is dead, if the supra-sensory world of the ideas has suffered the loss of its obligatory and above it its vitalizing and upbuilding power, then nothing more remains to which man can cling and by which he can orient himself." Heidegger is renowned also for a lot of his stuff being difficult to follow. This might explain why he said: "Making itself intelligible is suicide for philosophy." This hint at elitism may indicate why he was a Nazi supporter.

Perhaps he was a man after Averroes, who thought the common man should not concern himself with the subtleties of philosophy, which help interpret the religious beliefs of Islam. They should stick to the strict literalism of the Qur'anic text. If they were around today, both Averroes and Heidegger would get into serious trouble with the UK's Equality and Human Rights Commissioner. Ofsted might also have something to say about this non-educational approach.

[Figure: Sepia portrait drawing of Gilbert Ryle]

Ryle, Gilbert

1900 to 1976
Language, Phenomenology, Analytic

Gilbert Ryle began and ended at the seaside. He was born in the south of England, at Brighton and, 76 years later, died in the north at Whitby.

When it came to philosophy, Gilbert was definitely not all at sea. His main interest was in language, like Wittgenstein. He thought philosophical issues could be dealt with by consideration of the subtle uses of ordinary language.

His main work was "The Concept of Mind." Of which he said: "..could be described as a sustained essay in phenomenology, if you are at home with that label." One famous phrase in this book is: "The ghost in the machine." Here Gilbert was rejecting Descartes, mind – body dualism, where the mind was separate from the brain.

For Gilbert this was wrong, the mind and human consciousness was dependent on the brain, not separate from it. He refers to this Cartesian dualism as a category mistake, meaning you cannot put the mind in the same category as the physical brain. The mind is not some sort of substance. Mind and matter are different things, according to Gilbert. He went on to claim that the right use of words like 'thought' and 'mind' is in relation to human behaviour, meaning that mental processes are not distinct from observable behaviours. Philosophers are renowned for inventing an ism, or supporting one. Gilbert was unusual in that he disliked any of his philosophy being given an ism label.

[Figure: Colour photograph of Karl Popper in a blue jumper]

Popper, Karl

1902 to 1994 CE
Critical Rationalism, falsification

Karl was an Austrian who lived through two world wars. Apart from beating Democritus and pushing Russell for the honour of the longest lived great philosopher (eight years short of spanning three centuries), he is also known as the man threatened by Wittgenstein's poker.

In philosophy, his focus was the philosophy of science. He rejected classical inductionism (see Hume). His approach is termed empirical falsification. This

is also known as critical rationalism (philosophers are irritating with their use of terminology which is not immediately understandable, accept to aficionados. Averroes and Heidegger types permeate the philosophy club.)

Popper was the first to use this approach to objective knowledge. In essence falsification means conducting experiments to test a theory but if the outcome fails to support the theory, Popper says don't then cheat and try to amend the outcome. This is what he called falsification. This seems a little obvious, but Popper knows how attached philosophers and scientists can become to a pet idea. He considered that both scientific theory, and broadly human knowledge, couldn't get beyond a point at which it is conjectural. An example of his falsification approach he gave as: "While there is no way to prove that the sun will rise, it is possible to formulate the theory that every day the sun will rise; if it does not rise on some particular day, the theory will be falsified and will have to be replaced by a different one. Until that day, there is no need to reject the assumption that the theory is true." In support of this type of example he said: "In so far as a scientific statement speaks about reality, it must be falsifiable; and in so far as it is not falsifiable, it does not speak about reality." He thought that scientific advancement was evolutionary. Interestingly, he supported Einstein in his attack on Niels Bohr and the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. Time has shown that Karl has certainly lost out on that argument. While he admired, the German born Einstein, he was not at all enamoured by the German Nazi philosopher Heidegger:

Ayn Rand (born Alisa Rosenbaum)

1905 to 1982
Objectivism, ethical selfishness

There are three things unusual about Ayn Rand. First, she was born a Russian Jew and lived under communism. Second up, Ayn invented a new ism, 'Objectivism'. Her final uncommonality is that she was a woman, one of only a small number of female philosophers, and the only one with a Russian, and later an American émigré pedigree.

Ayn was born in 1905, in St Petersburg, then a major city of the Russian Empire. Twelve years later came the Bolshevik October Revolution.

This heralded the rise of communism and the Soviet Union. During this period her family life was disrupted when her father’s business was confiscated. Not long after graduating from Petrograd University, where she was introduced to Aristotle, she travelled to New York, to stay with relatives. Ayn found the New York skyline awe inspiring. She became enamoured of the American way of life, particularly the freedom and opportunities people had. This is not surprising given the rigid, restrictive communist system she had come from.

She determined to stay in America and use her writing skills in the entertainment industry. So, moving on to Hollywood, she became both a

[Figure: Film poster of "The Fountainhead" starring Gary Cooper and Patricia Neal]

scriptwriter and novelist. One of her best-selling books, “The Fountainhead,” was made into a film starring Gary Cooper and Patricia Neal.  Ayn wrote the script.

The film explored some of Ayn’s radical philosophical ideals founded on the tension between individualism (self-interest) and collectivism (common interest).  Her philosophical thoughts were further illustrated in another bestseller, a massive 1,163-page novel, “Atlas Shrugged.”

Ayn’s “Objectivism”, could be most simply described as the philosophy of out-and-out selfishness.  She described it like this: "My philosophy, in essence, is the concept of man as a heroic being, with his own happiness as the moral purpose of his life, with productive achievement as his noblest activity, and reason as his only absolute." Look out for yourself first is Ayn’s message. You have the choice to be lazy or productive.

She thought people could love or value others, but only if they were judged worth it: “Man should have self-esteem. …Love others for their virtues and values.” She proved she could love and be loyal through her single marriage. Frank O’Connor was her one and only husband for 50 years, until his death in 1979. One other point she made was that other people should not be forced, nor should you accept them forcing you.

She strongly challenged altruism and the idea, promoted by many religions and other institutions, that people should help others. This is the antithesis of Ayn’s doctrine: “Man working for others makes him a sacrificial animal.”

She was an atheist and said morality should be based on reason, not faith. Reason, she said was the absolute and should be the only guide to human thought and action, something after both Socrates and Kant. Ayn’s philosophy was initially rejected by academics, but has resurfaced in recent times, partly through the efforts of the Ayn Rand Institute, a non-profit organisation.

Sartre, Jean-Paul

1905 to 1980 CE
Existentialism, Phenomenology

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Jean-Paul Sartre seated, wearing round glasses and a suit]

Jean-Paul, a Frenchman, was good with the written word. He demonstrated this quite clearly through his capability in several literary fields as a: philosopher, playwright, novelist, screenwriter, biographer and literary critic.  His prowess in literature was formally recognised with the award of the Nobel Prize in 1964 but he refused it saying that no author should be turned into an institution. A darling of the left in politics, he was throughout his life a committed socialist, anti-fascist and anti-imperialist.  In his student days, he was quite a prankster, with a keen sense of the absurd in human life.

His philosophy was a form of existential phenomenology. He considered it essential to understand human existence (existentialism) rather than take great notice of the world itself. He tried to determine what it is to be human, focusing on the radical freedom of humans, their choices to be themselves. For J-P, our actions are not pre-determined. Following up on this J-P went on to say: and “Man is condemned to be free; because once thrown into the world, he is responsible for everything he does.” This freedom is the opposite of the theory, accepted since Plato and Aristotle, that we are born with an essential essence.

His great work “Being and Nothingness” explored these concepts alongside the difficulties to consider of consciousness.  J-Ps sense of humour, sometimes coupled with despair, shone through in his serious philosophical musings: "If I became a philosopher, if I have so keenly sought this fame for which I'm still waiting, it's all been to seduce women basically." and "Ah! yes, I know: those who see me rarely trust my word: I must look too intelligent to keep it." Jean-Paul also received the accolade of being the subject of a 1973 Monty Python sketch which ends:  Mrs Premise: "Jean-Paul. Your famous trilogy 'Rues i Liberté', is it an allegory of man's search for commitment?" Jean-Paul: "Oui". He also found time to be a political activist and get very close to the feminist philosopher Simone De Beauvoir from 1929 until he died. He held a view on music, at first saying it was irrelevant. Later he changed his tune acknowledging that jazz, at least, could represent his ideas of freedom and authenticity. On religion, he was for almost his entire life clearly an atheist. This position was founded on his existentialism. He put it, “existence precedes essence.” By this he meant purpose, or essence comes second and we, our existence with its freedom is the start point. Meaning by this that man is nothing else but what he makes of himself because there is no God involved in the design of man. Curiously though, the idea that man has free will is a key

issue for the debate over why God allows evil. Some theologians claim that God allows humans to freely choose between good and evil.

J-P was a reluctant atheist though and just before his death he said this, according to his friend Pierre Victor: “I do not feel that I am the product of chance, a speck of dust in the universe, but someone who was expected, prepared, prefigured. In short, a being whom only a Creator could put here; and this idea of a creating hand refers to God.” This statement was much to the dismay of his partner of 50 years, Simone De Beauvoir.

It is almost a de-facto requirement that philosophers should have strong disagreements, often with contemporaries, so just as Wittgenstein raged at Popper and Popper expressed his hatred of Heidegger, Jean-Paul angrily argued with Camus. Now, whose views do the modern world think carry more weight, Camus or Sartre? Well, The Guardian newspaper writer Stuart Jeffries thinks Sartre should still be listened to. In his article of 22 October 2014: "The existential plight of humanity, our absurd lot, our moral and political responsibilities that Sartre so brilliantly identified have not gone away; rather, we have chosen the easy path of ignoring them. " But one key word here is ‘absurd’ and Camus is the king of absurdism. So, is this article actually supporting both Sartre and Camus?

Arendt, Hannah

1906 to 1975 CE
Woman, Political

[Figure: Black and white portrait photograph of Hannah Arendt]

Hannah was in a somewhat similar mould to Mary Wollstonecraft. Both women advocated a liberal philosophy that laid heavy emphasis on equality and individual freedom. Both were unafraid to court controversy. In Hannah's case, she caused a storm of protest when claiming Eichmann, a Nazi chief, was not intrinsically evil. She coined a phrase that was not properly understood by some: "The banality of evil." Hannah explained what she meant by this in her book “The Human Condition” (1958) saying:

"It is, in fact, far easier to act under conditions of tyranny than it is to think."

She said of Eichmann he was a weak, mistaken man who was simply following orders.  Hannah saw this type of issue through a different lens than Mary's feministic emphasis. In her view, the rise of Nazi and Stalinist totalitarian states were examples that threatened individual political freedom.

For her some more modern political developments, which sought to control, were also a threat to "real" political liberalism. She lived through two world wars and was in Germany at the time of Hitler and Nazism.

These experiences and her affair with the Nazi philosopher, Martin Heidegger, must have had some influence on her political philosophy.  What did she advocate exactly? Hannah thought that people must have some type of open forum where the cross fertilisation of their individual views and their actions allowed a true consensus to emerge. This sort of idea goes back more than 2,000 years to the time of Socrates and the debates that took place in the forum of Athens. Well, democracy and liberalism, of sorts, did begin with the ancient Greeks although it did not save Socrates from the hemlock.

Merleau-Ponty, Maurice

1908 to 1961 CE
Existentialism, Phenomenology

[Figure: Black and white portrait photograph of Maurice Merleau-Ponty]

French philosophers seem to have been on a roll in the early 20th century. Not only was there Sartre, we have Merleau-Ponty, De Beauvoir, Camus and Foucault too. Maurice was influenced by Husserl and Heidegger, rather than the others, but he must have been aware of the work of his contemporaries. He believed we perceive the world through our whole body, not just through our consciousness. Both Descartes and Kant were wrong, said Maurice, because they unlatched the conscious person from the world of experience. He said:  ".... there is no inner man, man is in the world, and only in the world does he know himself."  One of the greats of 20th century philosophy and in modern times increasingly influential in the field of psychology. His main work was “Phenomenology of Perception.”

Unlike many of his contemporaries, Maurice did not ignore science, nor was he dismissive of it. He thought science was a contributory approach, though at a second level, to a full understanding of our world. In his view science was not simply a cold, calculating method of arriving at knowledge. Maurice considered there needed to be a continuous consideration of the information new science provided in helping move towards a full understanding.

He stressed that science was only a factor on the road to this understanding and not the sole route. His view of the secondary role of science is seen in:

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: Maurice Merleau-Ponty, source not named in the text, about 4 printed lines, beginning "Science manipulates things and gives up" and ending "only at rare intervals."]

and in the greater importance of philosophy: “Philosophy is not the reflection of a pre-existing truth, but, like art, the act of bringing truth into being.”

He said more interesting things:  "As a matter of principle, humanity is precarious: each person can only believe what he recognizes to be true internally and, at the same time, nobody thinks or makes up his mind without already being caught up in certain relationships with others, which leads him to opt for a particular set of opinions." The latter certainly supports the idea that the greatest reason for people’s particular religious views is " acceptance" (see the "Why a God" chapter).

De Beauvoir, Simone

1908 to 1986 CE
Woman, Existentialism

[Figure: Black and white portrait photograph of Simone de Beauvoir smiling]

Simone would probably have got on well with Mary Wollstonecraft, had they not been separated by more than a century. Both held strong feminist views and promoted women's equality with men. Unfortunately for Simone her place in history is often referenced to her role as the woman at the side of a man, Jean-Paul Sartre.

Even in death, she is next to JP.  They are buried in the same grave at Montparnasse. Like J-P she was an existentialist.

She used her other half's arguments in his Being and Nothingness to get at the core of relations between men and women.  In her work "The Second Sex"

Her book was important enough to be banned by the Vatican. Simone said that a woman: "...is defined and differentiated with reference to man and not he with her, she is incidental, the inessential, as opposed to the essential. He is the Subject; he is the Absolute - she is the Other." A bit of Hegel in this. De Beauvoir thought women were often their own worst enemies in the fight for equality in that they accepted their subjugation. This is very much along the same lines as Wollstonecraft. Simone's views are at the heart of today's sex equality debate in most Western societies.

So perhaps, after all she can be seen to have had a more practical, lasting impact than her famous partner. In future years maybe Jean-Paul will be referred to as the man next to Simone in that Montparnasse cemetery. In essence, J-P’s non-existence will be preceded by Simone’s.

To understand the working man better she gave up a teaching post and spent one year as a factory worker. Pacifism, she thought, was best served by joining an anarchist contingent on the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War. This did not last long because her comrades were worried that with her extreme short-sightedness she might accidentally shoot one of them. Her attachment and concern for the plight of her fellow man underpinned her thoughts and her actions for the whole of her short life, she explained why: “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.”

With Simone, you got exactly what it said on the tin. But you first had to read the small print carefully, e.g.

She was a Catholic, who did not believe in the Catholic sacrament of baptism, nor in the Catholic version of God;
She was a pacifist who thought it right to use a rifle, in certain circumstances;
Her version of communism required her to condemn some Marxists and to argue with Trotsky;
She believed in God, but also said it was no problem if he did not exist (although she explained this was entirely to do with our inability to fully understand all, as God did).

From this, it can be seen that Simone offered a slightly sideways view of the traditional Biblical God. This may be something to do with her background steeped in mysticism and Marxist purism. All this she combined with a general belief in a supreme being.

Simone was seemingly not wholly committed to the idea of God saying: “I should betray the truth . . . . if I left the point, where I have been since my birth, at the intersection of Christianity and everything that is not Christianity.” That sounds a bit agnostic, but it’s clear from her writings that Simone did believe in a God, just not the one so promoted by the Catholic church, for example she said:

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: Simone Weil, source not named in the text, about 7 printed lines, beginning "..the beauty of the world, …..the pure" and ending "keeps me outside the Church..."]

and “There are two atheisms of which one is a purification of the notion of God.”, finally, and perhaps most intriguingly:

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: Simone Weil, source not named in the text, about 3 printed lines on this page (the quotation continues on the next page), beginning "A case of contradictories which are true." and ending "my love is not illusory."]

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: Simone Weil, continuing from the previous page, about 4 printed lines, beginning "I am quite sure that there" (the quotation begins "A case of contradictories" on p.372) and ending "is not an illusion."]

Adding to this thought: “ "There is a trans-discursive, inconceivable reality." She is saying here something after the fashion of Einstein who described the impossibility of understanding God through his allegory of a child in a library. But hers is an original and difficult idea, that God both exists and does not exist, because we humans are not capable of knowing a true reality.  Simone’s God was one who did not get closely involved with humans. He left us to get on with it. It was God who was constrained while we had free will, she argued.

Simone was eloquent, if tricky to understand, on the subject of affliction and suffering. It's not clear whether she was suffering because afflicted or afflicted because of her suffering.  Sadly, Simone died quite young, aged 34, of a combination of tuberculosis and starvation. It's debatable whether she deliberately starved herself or whether her TB made her unable to eat.

Camus, Albert

1913 to 1960 CE
Existentialism, Absurdism

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Albert Camus with a cigarette, collar turned up]

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Humphrey Bogart with a cigarette]

Not often revealed of Camus, if at all, is his likeness to Humphrey Bogart (American film star of the 40's and 50's). This is Bogart bottom left. Perhaps Albert admired Bogart and was a fan of The African Queen? This film might have symbolised for Albert a long, difficult journey with a brave ending, who knows! Unfortunately, Albert's ending was more tragic than brave. He died in a car accident at the comparatively young age of 46.

Apart from his stand-in potential as a Bogart look-a-like, he managed to make a good living due to his many talents as a writer. In this regard, he could challenge his friend and protagonist, Jean-Paul Sartre. Camus' list of jobs included: journalist, editor and editorialist, playwright and director, novelist and author of short stories, political essayist and activist, and arguably, although he came to deny it, he was a philosopher.  Like Sartre, Albert was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature, but unlike his compatriot and rival, he accepted. In several areas the two intellectual giants of their age were apart, Camus was anti-communist while Sartre was pro. Camus was seen as the great moralist of his time.

He had a rather gloomy, dispiriting basis for his philosophy, that of considering the question of suicide as a fundamental issue for philosophy. It’s absurd to seek meaning in life when there is none and it’s absurd to attempt to understand the world, so argued Camus. He thought it impossible to gain rational knowledge: “That universal reason, practical or ethical, that determinism, those categories that explain everything are enough to make a decent man laugh” In this he set himself against both science and philosophy.

These were not the only things he was against. His political views were neither of the far left or capitalist right.  He set up the Group for International Liaisons specifically to: "denounce two ideologies found in both the USSR and the USA".  His existentialism has a strong dash of absurdism. Of course, he did not accept being labelled as an existentialist and being put alongside his rival Sartre.

So, he seemed to be against philosophy, against life, against capitalism, against communism, and against science. He also appeared to have strong anti-establishment feelings.

One thing he was not against was being honoured by the award of the Nobel prize, this, from a very establishment institution. Does this make Albert a tiny bit of a hypocrite? No, that’s absurd!

Ayer, A.J.

Sir Alfred Jules, “Freddie”
1910 to 1989 CE
Logical positivism

[Figure: Black and white photograph of A.J. Ayer smiling, in a suit and tie]

Freddie was better known as A.J. He was renowned as a charmingly clever man who loved football, films and women. An Eton boy, he graduated from Christ Church, Oxford and later taught at Oxford University. A.J. eventually acceded to the Wykeham Chair of logic. He was knighted for his services to education and philosophy. His lucidity and calmness when under pressure was illustrated when, in strained circumstances, he met Mike Tyson (one-time world heavyweight boxing champion).

At a New York party he heard a girl screaming that Tyson was assaulting a woman, the model Naomi Campbell, in a bedroom. A.J. confronted Tyson who said: "Do you know who.....I am?...  I'm the heavyweight boxing champion of the world." Ayer calmly and politely replied: " And I am the former Wykeham professor of logic...., We are both pre-eminent in our field I suggest we talk about this like rational men." During this conversation Naomi escaped.

What made his name in the philosophers' pantheon was his introduction of something called “logical positivism" to the English language. This turned up in his book: “Language, Truth and Logic.” Alfred claimed that any positive statement must either be analytic (obvious from the words) or be backed up by empirical evidence. This was the only way to verify such a statement. Thus, reasoned A.J., statements about moral or ethical issues are neither analytic or verifiable and so are meaningless. In effect, he said there is no such thing as right and wrong. Is that right? It cannot be, but it also cannot be wrong of course.

It is doubtful whether A.J.'s views cut much ice with mothers. Not being able to tell little Freddy or Emily that it's wrong to chuck food across the table would be quite a problem for them. And what about the impact on the religious establishment? A.J.’s views, saying there’s no right or wrong, could easily translate into contending there is no such thing as good and evil.  Widespread acceptance of such views would decimate some major religions.

He went on to say our perception of physical objects was heavily influences  by our senses. Many people might not see this in anyway a revolutionary idea.

His type of verification idea has more than a passing similarity with Karl Popper's falsification concept. No doubt these two came across each other’s work.  A.J. was not a believer in a supreme deity, he said:  "I do not believe in God. It seems to me that theists of all kinds have very largely failed to make their concept of a deity intelligible; and to the extent that they have made it intelligible, they have given us no reason to think that anything answers to it." He had a very clear moral standpoint, of inclusivity and fairness to all, without pointing to any godly source. For A.J. this is what should be the basis of our dealings with other people: "The only possible basis for a sound morality is mutual tolerance and respect: tolerance of one another’s customs and opinions; respect for one another’s rights and feelings; awareness of one another’s needs." He did not believe a God had to be involved if people were to have moral standards: “No morality can be founded on authority, even if the authority were divine.”
