Anscombe, Elizabeth

1919 to 2001 CE
Woman, Consequentialism, Virtue ethics

[Figure: Black and white portrait photograph of Elizabeth Anscombe]

Elizabeth, or Miss Anscombe as she was generally known, was a student of Wittgenstein at Cambridge. The Miss tag is deceptive. She married fellow philosopher Peter Geach and mothered 3 sons and 4 daughters. Not surprisingly, she was a devout Catholic and a strong opponent of contraception. Her personal morality also made her publicly criticise the award of an honorary Oxford degree to Harry Truman. She considered him a mass murderer for his decision to drop atom bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

Ludwig, who usually did not have a lot of time for women, admiringly, referred to her as "old man"! She was considered by some to be the greatest philosopher of her generation, perhaps that means discounting the period she overlapped with Wittgenstein, Popper, Sartre, Camus, Heidegger, De Beauvoir and Foucault.

Elizabeth was instrumental in bringing Ludwig's work to a world-wide audience through writing an introduction to Tractatus, translating

Philosophical Investigations and by her intelligent work as an executor. But Miss Anscombe made her own impact as a philosopher, quite separate from just as a follower and promoter of Wittgenstein. Her main work was "Intention". Fellow philosopher Donald Davidson said this showed the best reasoning since Aristotle, high praise. One of the few women philosophers. She invented consequentialism and arguably virtue ethics. Aristotle made emphasis on virtue but his was as a package towards ultimate good and happiness.

Elizabeth’s virtue ethics was a little different. It focussed on what kind of person someone should be and what list of virtues make for a moral life. Consequentialism sounds much deeper than it really is. It simply means the consequences of whatever we choose to do are the final basis for any decision about the rightness or wrongness of our conduct. You might think this smacks of inconsequentialism rather than the opposite. Perhaps Elizabeth would have been better off if she had stuck to the task of uncovering and championing Wittgenstein.

Foucault, Michel

1926 to 1984 CE
Post-Modernism

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Michel Foucault smiling, wearing glasses and a patterned jacket]

Michel Foucault (pronounced Foo-coo) was the son of a Poitiers surgeon and another off the production line of French 20th century philosophers. After studying with Maurice Merleau–Ponty he later taught at the universities of Uppsala, Hamburg and Warsaw. Michel was influenced by the German philosophers Heidegger and Nietzsche. His doctoral thesis was titled “Madness and Unreason: A History of Madness in the Classical Age”. This does not sound like a relaxing read on a sunny beach holiday.

Michel was not only a philosopher but also a historian of ideas and truth; a social theorist, philologist, literary critic and political activist. Towards the end of his life he said all the areas of his work and interest were intended to address one single issue, what he called the production of truth throughout history. He meant that at different stages in history different truths were accepted and power was wielded based on these generally accepted truths, this is something like Protagoras’ view of subjective perception. An example would be the Catholic inquisition which held that the Earth was the centre of the universe. Galileo, Copernicus and Giordano Bruno suffered for failing to accept this particular "truth".

Michel explained: " I set out to grasp the mechanisms of the effective exercise of power; and I do this because those who are inserted in these relations of power, who are implicated therein, may, through their actions, their resistance, and their rebellion, escape them, transform them—in short, no longer submit to them." He claimed that power is everywhere. That seems too obvious to be worth stating but Foucault thinks that the usual concept of power is incorrect. He believes his approach, though a critical history of modernity (his words) shows that power is found in all interactions and relationships. Accepted truth implies knowledge and is associated with the use of power.

He also thought schools were just regulatory institutions: “Schools serve the same social functions as prisons and mental institutions - to define, classify, control, and regulate people.” Well, Michel surely this depends on the school? Don’t some, at least, educate their pupils and prepare them quite well for adult life? He died of HIV.

Derrida, Jacques

1930 to 2004 CE
Deconstructionism, Post-modernism

[Figure: Black and white portrait photograph of Jacques Derrida]

A Frenchman born in Algeria, before its independence. Jacques has caused a great kerfuffle in later 20th century philosophical circles. He claimed he was not a philosopher because philosophy was impossible. Jacques was influenced by Husserl's phenomenology and Heidegger’s concept of being. Maybe he tried to compete with these two in the philosophers' top division of "difficult to understand" league. Jacques was one of those pessimistic types, understandable then that he suffered several bouts of depression. Was he depressed because of what appear to be thoughts on the hopelessness of trying to understand anything, or was it his depression that gave him such thoughts? A chicken and egg situation here. He based his thoughts on the idea we could not really get to the absolute truth of anything through either philosophy or science. This, he seemed to claim (using "seemed" because Jacques is notoriously difficult to understand) was because our speech and language was not capable of expressing a true reality.

He claimed we were all about perceptions and differing mental interpretations of the same words. Leaning quite a lot on Wittgenstein here.

Before getting into his main philosophical idea, here’s a Derrida quote which suggests he did not believe in a heaven, and ergo he did not believe in an Abrahamic God: “Learning to live ought to mean learning to die - to acknowledge, to accept, an absolute mortality - without positive outcome, or resurrection, or redemption, for oneself or for anyone else. That has been the

old philosophical injunction since Plato: to be a philosopher is to learn how to die.” An odd comment this, among many that he made. If there is one thing that is an absolute certainty, we do not need to learn how to die. It is going to happen regardless of any degree of learning. Of course, probably Derrida did not intend his comment to be taken quite so literally. He possibly meant to suggest that Epicurus’ advice should be followed - death is nothing to fear.

Derrida’s fame is not because of his deadly remarks. It’s because he came up with a new ism - deconstructionism. Deconstructionism, things are way beyond their elementary components, that’s the truth of it, or is there any truth Derrida might say. He was also lauded with being a type of post-modernist. His own thinking, if you accept he is right, must be subject to doubt.

His thoughts were controversial and this was clearly demonstrated by the debate surrounding his award of an honorary degree by Cambridge University. Many dons opposed this award. In a letter to The Times this was said:

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: Cambridge dons opposing Derrida's honorary degree, letter to The Times, about 6 printed lines, beginning "His works employ a written style" and ending "either false or trivial."]

[Figure: Photograph of an elderly Derrida with a quotation: "Deconstruction never had meaning or interest, at least in my eyes, than as a radicalization, that is to say, also within the tradition of a certain Marxism, in a certain spirit of Marxism." — Jacques Derrida — AZ QUOTES]

Some other quotes by Derrida: "For this is what I hold and what in turn holds me in its grip, the aleatory strategy of someone who admits that he does not know where he is going." Does this point to some self-doubt? Is he thinking of Socrates:  “I know that I know nothing.”?

He also said:

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: Jacques Derrida, source not named in the text, about 7 printed lines, beginning "When I say that this phase" and ending "is never a dead letter."]

The latter is an example of the difficulty of understanding him, for some of us. Here’s another: “That is what deconstruction is made of: not the mixture but the tension between memory, fidelity, the preservation of something that has been given to us, and, at the same time, heterogeneity, something absolutely new, and a break.” Just try and pick the bones out of Jacques comment above. Was Jacques so clever and tortuously correct that very few, if any, could fully appreciate him, or was he a supreme intellectual conman? It is quite possible he did not fully understand himself and so chose to hide behind complex and seemingly meaningless statements. This certainly would explain why he had such difficulty in clearly making his views understood, but perhaps this is being unfair to Jacques. One just needs a bigger brain, even bigger than those Cambridge dons who said his writings are incomprehensible.

Plantinga, Alvin

Nov. 1932 to?
Analytic

[Figure: Photograph of Alvin Plantinga laughing, white-bearded, wearing glasses and a white shirt]

Alvin is best known for his analytic philosophy in defence of religion. He's written much on this topic including: “God and Other Minds”, “God, Freedom and Evil” and “Warranted Christian Belief”. For his efforts, he was awarded the Templeton Prize in 2017 (made for exceptional contribution to life's spiritual aspect). The awarding committee said about him: "an American scholar whose rigorous writings over a half century have made theism - the belief in a divine reality or god - a serious option within academic philosophy." Richard Dawkins has been critical of this award commenting that it's made:  "usually to a scientist who is prepared to say something nice about religion".

In answering questions about why God does not make it clear that he exists Alvin claims atheists have something akin to a disease which prevents them freely accepting, in the way Calvin correctly, apparently did, that God exists. He says "due to the entry of sin into the world sometimes our cognitive facilities  don't function the way they should." Well, whom was it religious people claim invented intelligent humans? Why didn't He ensure their brains always fired on all cylinders? What seems to have occurred, identified consistently in frequent surveys, is that atheists are more intelligent on average than religious people.  It’s quite a mystery why God, assuming there is one, allowed this to happen, surely, he would want his believers to have the most brain power.

Alvin also appears to offer some challengeable statements. For instance, he said God would want us to know about him. If this is so, why does He not make this crystal clear and so avoid the situation where there are many millions of non-believers. The super-powerful God could easily override the unbelievers faulty minds, as claimed by Plantinga (see chapter, God - The Biggest Question?).

On the question of evidence for the existence of God’s  he said:

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: Alvin Plantinga, source not named in the text, about 5 printed lines, beginning "But lack of evidence, if indeed" and ending "instead be agnosticism."]

What! Does this mean Alvin is an agnostic when it comes to God?

And then commenting on the perennial issue of why a kind and loving God allows evil to exist. There is a lot of debate over the question of evil. Alvin comes up with a clever but difficult answer to why God allows it to exist. He argues that evil is linked to its opposite, i.e. goodness. Alvin says God could not get rid of evil without also eliminating goodness. In essence, he says evil can logically exist if God has granted humans free will.  They are free to be good or to commit evil. Interestingly he does not claim his argument proves the case for God’s existence, only that it is logically possible.  Therefore, the existence of evil is ambivalent to the God issue. It does not prove God does not exist, nor does it prove he does exist.

It is possible to ask serious questions about both evil and free will. Is it really in the power of an omnipotent (all-powerful) and omniscient (all knowing) being to allow real free will? Schopenhauer did not think so.

“Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills”.
(Schopenhauer mainly rejects the idea of free-will, arguing that actions are determined by things that don’t change: motives, incentives and character.)

How does freewill sit with God as an omniscient entity? Everything we think, say and do is based on a number of factors: genetic make-up, inheritance, circumstances, culture, environment, desires, interaction with others, health and mind influencing substances. In short, our thoughts and actions are governed by the entire world, and universe around us, past and present.

The omnipotent entity that is God is the one who set up the entire environment which embraces and determines our whole existence. If we could gather all

the relevant factors then input them into an enormous and hyper-fast computer it could calculate our future thoughts and actions. God is that hyper-computer. HE can work out what we end up doing and whether we will be morally good or bad. In essence, everything about humans is therefore pre-determined, assuming the Abrahamic God exists. This dichotomy between freewill and a determined universe is known as incompatibilism.  In addition to this, it’s claimed that God is omniscient (all-knowing) This means God knows what we are going to think, say and do before we know it ourselves. HE’s known this forever.  So, how does omnipotence and omniscience fit with free will? Can God somehow close his eyes or switch off knowing? These points were made in Chapter 3, under the morality heading, but they are so fundamentally important they are worthy of another mention. We also recognise that religious theologians claim God has another key attribute, omnibenevolence (moral perfection).

Evil and moral perfection are uneasy bedfellows, no matter the clever arguments. The existence of evil remains disturbing in the God argument, as Alvin himself admits.

TIME magazine called Alvin: "America's leading orthodox Protestant philosopher of God." In his belief Alvin is among a minority in philosophers. Commenting on Alvin's interview by Gary Gutting in 1994, Professor of Philosophy Massimo Pigliucci said: "..the proportion of atheists among academic philosophers is at around 62%, slightly above what it is for scientists.” Alvin concedes that this outcome is problematic for theism, considering that philosophers are the ones who are most familiar with all the arguments for and against the theistic position. So, what does he do? He quotes Richard Dawkins, quoting Bertrand Russell, who famously said that if he found himself in front of God after his death he would point out to him,” there just wasn’t enough evidence." David Chalmers and David Bourget conducted a wide-ranging survey of philosophers and students of philosophy in 2014. They found 72% were atheists, a 21% increase on those quoted by Pigliucci.

Singer, Peter

1946 to?
Ethics

[Figure: Photograph of Peter Singer resting his chin on his hand, wearing glasses]

Here we have an Australian philosopher. Peter was born and worked in Melbourne before he became Professor of Bioethics at Princeton University, USA.

Peter is probably best known for his campaign and philosophy concerning animal welfare. His book “Animal Liberation” was

first published in 1975. In this he condemns the ill-treatment of animals by humans, referring to this as speciesist.  He says animals are capable of much suffering and we humans ignore this because they are not human.

Arthur Schopenhauer was an early proponent of Peter Singer’s position: “The assumption that animals are without rights and the illusion that our treatment of them has no moral significance is a positively outrageous example of Western crudity and barbarity. Universal compassion is the only guarantee of morality.”

Peter has shown his capacity to be controversial, not only with his claims about animals but also on subjects such as abortion and euthanasia, both of which he supports. He adopts a utilitarian approach, after the fashion of Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

He argues that with abortion the question is what is the mother’s preference and what the foetus. Since, he says, the foetus has no capacity to experience the sensations of either suffering or satisfaction the mother’s wants are paramount. He went further than this claiming that up to about 18 weeks old babies “..lack the essential characteristics of personhood.” He describes these features as "rationality, autonomy, and self-consciousness".  Then he argued, a little sensationally: “killing a new-born baby is never equivalent to killing a person, that is, a being who wants to go on living."

There were some calls by disability activists for him to resign over this remark of his: “….if a decision is taken, by the parents and doctors, that it is better that a baby should die, I believe it should be possible to carry out that decision, not only by withholding or withdrawing life support — which can lead to the baby dying slowly from dehydration or from an infection — but also by taking active steps to end the baby’s life swiftly and humanely.”

Peter does not believe in the Judao/Christian God “I think we can be clear that being does not exist…..The world around us contains an immensity of suffering..,.I think this is a major stumbling block to belief in the Christian God.” Why would God create a world with such suffering, he says? The free will argument does not hold water according to Peter. He says there is lots of suffering in the world that is not the result of free will. This cannot be explained by free will. 1949 to?
Modern Scepticism, Humanism

[Figure: Photograph of A.C. Grayling with long hair and glasses]

Professor Grayling, A.C. as he is known, has an atheist, humanist and secularist basis for his philosophy.  He is a prolific writer. and communicator through modern media.  His philosophical interests embrace both technical aspects, shown by the thesis for his doctorate: “Epistemological Scepticism and Transcendental Arguments”. A.C. has also written: “Against All Gods: Six Polemics on Religion” and an “Essay on Kindness”.

In considering practical ethics he poses what he refers to as the great Socratic question: "How should one live?'. " Answering his own question he said "..contributing to the conversation society has with itself about possibilities for good lives in good societies." A.C. contributes on a wide range of contemporary issues:  the legalisation of drugs, euthanasia, secularism, and human rights and on war crimes.

In his book The God Argument A.C. argues cogently against the idea of a God addressing the intelligent design, cosmological, moral and ontological attempted proofs. A.C. concludes: “The cumulative case against religion shows it to be a hangover from the infancy of modern humanity, persistent and enduring because of the vested interests of religious organisations…..” and “…..it is one of the most destructive forces plaguing humanity.” His views on religion and religious zealots are typified in his reaction to the killing of a British soldier, Lee Rigby, in Woolwich by Muslim converts Michael Adebolajo and Michael Adebowale. A.C. said:

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: A.C. Grayling, on the killing of Lee Rigby, source not named in the text, about 5 printed lines, beginning "Belief in supernatural beings, miracles and" and ending "justifies believers in what they do."]

[Quotation still to be typed in from the printed book: A.C. Grayling, continuing the same passage, about 4 printed lines, beginning "Unnatural lifestyles, self-harm, ritualistic repetitive" and ending "the result is dangerous."]

and "Dogma will always lead to murder. In the end, scepticism is the only answer."

Although clearly having no truck with religion’s claims of a God he is content that people should be free to believe whatever they wish with one important condition: “People should be left to believe what they like, so long as they harm no one else.". Voltaire said something very similar almost 300 years before A.C.

Humanism is offered up by A.C. as a positive alternative to follow away from religion; “Humanism is above all about living thoughtfully and intelligently, about rising to the demand to be informed, alert and responsive, about being able to make a sound case for a choice of values and goals…..”

A.C. is Vice-President of Humanists UK (see Chapter 22, What Else if Not Religion?). He could be seen as a philosopher who addresses the everyday issues that concern people. A philosopher who other philosophers can appreciate and whom the general public, who may be dismissive of philosophy, can identify with. The Times said: “While most philosophy is written in abstruse and ponderous prose, Grayling’s is a model of clarity and elegance.”

Notes and acknowledgements:

(1) The above 104 are just a slice of the many philosophers who we know of and who have populated planet Earth for the past 2,500 years. There are others but this is my selection of important philosophers.

(2) The comments by no means reflect the full scope of each philosopher’s background, writings or utterances.  They are a snapshot of a far bigger picture. I've tried to keep things fairly short by picking out what to me are the key ideas and arguments, expressing them mostly in my own terms.

(3) Inevitably, this is a subjective exercise.  All the content is arguable, without question, but contention is a defining feature of all philosophy and all philosophers, so that's all right!

(4) Main sources of information:  Wikipedia; Wikiquotes; the Internet Encyclopaedia of Philosophy;  Stanford University Encyclopaedia of Philosophy; Paul Strathern's audiobooks Philosophy in an Hour;  DK's The Philosophy Book;  The Independent, The Great Philosophers series; Stephen Law's The Great Philosophers and Philosophy; Philosophy A Graphic Guide and Introducing Philosophy by Dave Robinson and Judy Groves; Richard Popkin and Avrum Stroll's Philosophy Made Simple; Lesley Levene’s I Think Therefore I am; Marcus Weeks Philosophy in Minutes and Bryan Magee's The Great Philosophers. BBC Radio 4, In Our Time. I'm grateful to all these sources for revealing the mysteries of philosophy and the astonishing thoughts of the great philosophers.  Nigel Blackmore November 2020

Personal Philosophy

A definition of philosophy has already been given earlier. We know from this that it covers a wide range of topics. But my suggestion here is focused solely on an ethical philosophy. This to enable people to be:

Fit For Life

Even people who claim complete ignorance of philosophy or those who are contemptuous of it have a philosophy of their own. They do not necessarily know this. Nor would some feel comfortable about having it pointed out, but it is so. The Oxford Dictionary describes philosophy as: “The study of the fundamental nature of knowledge, reality, and existence.” Now this sounds quite deep and lacking in the mundane of how most people go about their lives. Few spend much time pondering the metaphysical issue of “the fundamental nature of reality”. Yet the Dictionary, helpfully, goes on to give a more prosaic explanation of philosophy: “A theory or attitude that acts as a guiding principle for behaviour.” We are in business with this description.

Everyone has some sort of outlook on life that determines their thoughts, speech and behaviour in certain circumstances. This simply means that people have opinions or reactions which underpin their attitude to politics; finance; leisure; relationships with family, friends, other people, religion, and other things. In the same fashion, they can iterate their choice with vitally important questions (to some of us) such as what is the rugby side the manager should pick. Everyone can back up their opinions with argument and reasoning, no matter how instinctive or shallow this might sometimes appear. This is a form of philosophy. Often, the basic, underlying personal rules or steers that people use, sometimes completely unconsciously, is a type of ethical philosophy.

My own ethical philosophy is very easily described here. You may be relieved to know, there is no “ism” claimed for it! And you don’t need to study Aristotle’s highly analytical approach set out in Nicomachean Ethics. You can if you want, but my words though less, much less, deep have the advantage of simplicity.  I try to keep to my own ethical philosophy but don’t always succeed. No matter, it is definitely FIT for purpose. Well, I would say that, wouldn’t I?

F is for fairness. This means treat your fellow man, or woman, with fairness and kindly consideration. If you treat others fairly they are more likely to reciprocate although not always.

Thinking of others and treating them well will help you feel at ease that you have done the right thing. You will have established an ethical, secure moral base for yourself. Being fair does not mean letting people trample all over you. Sometimes, being fair means making a comment or taking an action that you know may not be immediately appreciated.  For example, parents are not being fair to their children if they allow them to do exactly what they like. Such children will grow up to be selfish. They will not know the boundaries of behaviour and may find it harder to have friends.

It has been shown in scientific studies that humans have an innate concept of fairness which they apply (well, some do) for the benefit of others even though it may be slightly detrimental to themselves in the immediate term. Of course, this innateness is not an absolute imperative. Some people easily override it and are totally or mostly selfish.

I is for interest. Take an interest in a wide range of concrete things, people or knowledge. Be like Socrates who said the unquestioning mind is not worth living. Broad knowledge can make for a happier life. You have a wider range of things to become fascinated by. Boredom and dissatisfaction are defeated, because there is always something you are interested in and are pursuing. Having wide-ranging knowledge also helps with better decision making. You are unlikely to become a narrow-minded bigot or intolerant fanatic if you ask questions and have some broad knowledge of our amazing world, or even more, know something of our astounding universe. Remember what Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy author, Douglas Adams, said: “Let us think the unthinkable, let us do the undoable, let us prepare to grapple with the ineffable itself, and see if we may not eff it after all.” A bit tricky you think, doing the undoable? Perhaps Douglas simply meant make more of an effort pull up your stuck trouser zip otherwise you will be undone. And bear in mind, or maybe not, that his “F it” has a different derivation than the FIT I suggest.

T is for try. Try and achieve small tasks and bigger goals. Don’t let life drift on by. Do things and plan to do more things. Making the effort and then succeeding can give a comfortable, warm feeling. You will feel good having achieved something after battling though any difficulties and sticking to your task.  Even relative failure can be worthwhile and better than making no effort. It is certainly preferable to giving up too readily.

We can all learn from our mistakes. They can help point us in the right direction for another go at something. But don’t make a meal of it. You must not feel required to be always pursuing some worthy task or other. Relax and take it easy too. Get out occasionally into green countryside. It’s good for the psyche. Make time for leisure activities.  We are social beings, contact with people is very important, so visit or chat with friends and family. Join a club whose objectives cover something of interest to you. Do other things like reading a book, going out for a meal, playing on the computer or smart phone, attending a football match, cinema or theatre. These types of activities are as important as diligence in working towards a goal. Just don’t become either totally driven, hedonistic or lazy. The great Sir Terry Pratchett’s Discworld philosopher, Ly Tin Wheedle, says: “You have to do something or be considered, in the great scheme of things, a tit.” And remember, whatever you do or try to do, laughter is essential. It’s proven to be good for your health. So, make sure you laugh very regularly. (see Chapter 21 Design a God).

[Figure: Logo reading "Fit for Life" on a blue oval]

Finally, and perhaps most importantly of all, there’s no need to believe or follow me or indeed anyone else. As Michel de Montaigne said: “He who follows another follows nothing. He finds nothing; indeed, he seeks nothing.” You can admire or agree with the views of others but never, ever, be a blind, unthinking disciple. Ask probing questions, seek the evidence and consider alternatives. Peter Abelard made this point: "The first key to wisdom is assiduous and frequent questioning."

Never be led by the nose. Make up your own mind, always, but be tolerant of people who think differently to you.

So, there we have it, be FIT for life. With this approach, you set yourself in a good position to be happy and to enjoy life, as much as circumstances allow. You are also likely to make a positive contribution to human society generally.

Nigel Blackmore  2020

Some isms explained

Absurdism This basically says, everything is hopeless, there’s no point in trying to find meaning in life, that’s just daft, it’s absurd. See Camus.

Animism This is a sort of all-embracing Gaia concept, where all objects – animals, plants, humans, rocks the weather – are thought to have a spiritual essence. This essence can influence future events. It’s a belief that may have been common with pre-historic humans.

Aristotelianism The clue here is in the word, Aristotle. If you are a follower of this ism, it means you quite like what this guy has to say. Try Averroes or, of course, Aristotle himself.

Behaviourism There are several varieties of this, including psychological behaviourism, but we are concerned with the common philosophical type.  Here it’s to do with mind. Things in our mind, mental terms or concepts, can translate into behavioural terms and concepts, i.e. what people do as a result of a thought. Any mental state is directly linked to behaviour, so behaviourists claim. This theory is not so popular in modern philosophy.  Gilbert Ryle may be a behaviourist of sort.

Buddhism You don’t have to sit under a Bodhi tree to understand what this is all about. Study the four noble truths then follow the right path, the eight-fold one, and you will get there. Gautama tells all.

Conceptualism Universals can exist, but only inside your head mind. A sort of middle road between nominalism and realism. Abelard and Ockham of this type.

Confucianism Not to be confused with confusianism. Confucianism encourages humility and a sense of knowing-your-place. Confucius’s philosophy was very useful to Chinese rulers, guess why?

Constructivism No, this is not a disease that serial, high-rise builders suffer from. In philosophy it generally refers to a theory of knowledge. Constructivism, from an epistemological point of view, says people use their own experiences to build up a picture of well, everything they think they know and understand. Would this better be referred to as obviousism, but that would leave out reason and that’s not rational, is it?

Cynicism You are not going to believe this, so no point in saying what this is about. Antisthenes was the first cynic, “Oh yeah?” I hear you cynically say, but his student Diogenes was the one who gave it serious momentum.

Deconstructionism Something to do with knocking down old buildings you could surmise? You might be right, because even its chief, maybe sole, proponent, Derrida, could not clearly explain what this meant. Apparently, it’s related to the interface between text and meaning – if that means anything mind you.

Dualism This is not something to mind. It doesn’t really matter, although there’s a body of work that says it does. Have a look at Descartes.

Empiricism Was Queen Victoria an empiricist? She certainly lorded it, or should that be lady-ed it, over the British Empire. Her knowledge of this was based on common sense and experience, this is empiricism, David Hume is with Victoria as an empiricist.

Epicureanism You can have quite a good time getting to grips with this one, but I fear you have to learn a bit of Greek first: ataraxia and aponia. This is a pain, I know. No!  quite the opposite. Followers are Epicurus, naturally, and his Roman admirer Lucretius.

Essentialism Here we are born to be a certain thing which we may or may not achieve. It is the opposite of existentialism complete freedom. Plato and Aristotle were of this view.

Existentialism Jean Paul Sartre, in the 1940s, was this idea’s main proponent, but he did say he pursued his philosophy as a way of getting girls. Roughly, it says all we have, know and do is based on our own existence in the world. We find things out through free will and choice. This is a supremely true philosophy, to an extent. We definitely have to exist first before we can experience anything.

Fallibism Fallibism is quite useful in an argument. You can say, “I’m going to be fallibistic. I know I’m right, even though I can’t prove it.” Many have probably engaged in fallibism without knowing it.

Historicism What’s coming up now is because of what came up in the past.

Holism A bit psychological here: “The whole is greater than the parts.” Perhaps it should be wholism.

Humanism Humanists believe in non-belief. It is also a more positive stance towards the world, even to the universe, than their closely allied cousins, the atheists.  Humanists think of science almost as a God. Everything is natural and can be explained, with the help of science.  There is no need for the intervention of a deity, or any other supernatural entity, so say humanists. Grayling is one of these.

Incompatibilism Here we have maybe a cry for help from some religious inclined people. It recognises that it’s impossible to have a deterministic Godly approach – everything is pre-ordained – and freewill. The two don’t go together. They are incompatible. Help, what do we do if we want to have an omniscient, all capable God alongside humans who have freedom to decide whether to be goodies or badies. Along came Liberalism.

Idealism This assumes an order, mind and consciousness first, matter follows on and is secondary. But the universe had lots and lots of matter for a long time, before any mind or consciousness cranked into life, so this philosophy may not be ideal.

Immaterialism George Berkeley was very determined this one was correct. For George everything that we thought existed was simply our perception. It was all in the mind, aided by God.  This links closely with Idealism.

Infallibism This is so true, you cannot doubt it.

Instrumentalism No, it’s is  not a generic reference to the action of someone who plays the oboe or flute in an orchestra. John Dewey was enamored of it. Thought, he said quite pragmatically, it is just an instrument for solving practical problems. You might think that’s obvious.

Isimitis An essential contractible disease by philosophers. All seek to be associated with an original ‘ism’ like Diogenes with Cynicism and Plato with Platonism. If not the originator, important for philosophers to be associated with an ism that they add a few twists of their own to. These additions are sometimes so extensive the philosopher receives the accolade of establishing a neo-ism, such as Plotinus with Neo-Platonism.

Liberalism: No, this Liberalism is not referring to the key policy aim of the British political party, the Liberals. Well, in fact it is their underlying aim, but in philosophy of religion it can have two meanings.
First, it may refer to tolerance of other religions, or it can also refer to the idea of humans having free will. They can choose to be good or evil, it is said. Alleging that despite an all-knowing God etc, our thoughts, speech, and actions are not pre-ordained. See also essentialism and existentialism.

Materialism Opposite of immaterialism and idealism, materialism is where matter comes before mind. Well, our brains are made of matter and are a source of our consciousness, so maybe 5 out of 5 here. Materialist say everything is composed of matter. Thales and Democritus were early materialists. For Marx, materialism meant something different. It was bad, the quest for more and more and more was something those nasty capitalists were engaged in.  This one is a good points earner for philosophers, because it’s also a form of monism. Two isms at once result in a good score in the philosopher’s league.

Monism Constantly complaining would be moanism, close to monism, but not close enough. Monism is a recognition of a single source for things. The Eleatic school was keen on monism. All is one and one is all. Sounds like the script of a Three Musketeers movie. The Abrahamics are monists, whereas ancient Egyptians are certainly not. The former have just the one God, while the latter enjoyed thousands.

Nominalism An anti-term that in its most common usage says there’s no such thing as a universal something – that is, words that imply separate things have some group commonality. It’s anti-universals, those such as Plato’s Perfect Forms.

Non-cognitivism Don’t you understand this? Well, you are on the right track. In philosophy it’s usually an expression related to ethics. Non-cognitivism indicates that sometimes you have not got the complete picture. For example, saying a robbery is wrong is not, strictly, an ethical statement about morality. We have to go on to say why it is that robbery and any robbery is wrong, otherwise we are stuck in non-cognitivism. This is too abstruse for many of us, but philosophers enjoy this sort of thing.

Occasionalism Everything comes from God, Nicolas Malebranche said “there is only one true cause because there is only one true God.”, although he thought this was true all of the time, not just occasionally. Bishop Berekeley was one of these.

Objectivism Here we have a new-ish kid on the block. It is anti the build it up idea of constructionism. It says its already there, objective reality, is what it is, it does not change. You don’t need to construct it. There’s an ethical element too. It has four tenets: 1. Reality is what it is, e.g. the cosmos is there; 2. Reason is all that’s needed to understand all, don’t embrace faith; 3. Self-interest, in pursuit of happiness, but value others; 4. Capitalism, and its promotion of individual freedom. All this in the pursuit of self-happiness. Google Ayn Rand (1905-1982), or look at page 365.

Platonism, Neo-Platonism Platonists love Plato, only Platonically though. Any other form of love is impossible, given his nearly two and half millennia of deadness.  Neo-Platonists were a Johnny-come-lately lot. They were not satisfied with pure Platonism so added a few bits and pieces, from Christianity and Eastern mysticism. Plato’s thoughts, mainly from his dialogue Republic, were slightly re-jigged to bolster the religious views of Jews and Christians. Plotinus was the chief instigator of the neo-Platonic world, although he did not know this. There’s also a sort of halfway house, between the original Plato and the neo, a middle Platonism.

Pluralism This expression has not just one meaning, monism or two meanings, dualism. It has at least three! The most common usage of pluralism, in philosophy, is in reference to politics, usually western politics. In the main it says, let lots of people’s voices be heard; an expression of democracy. It can also point to a theory that there are more than one or two ultimate realities.  Finally, it is a societal term saying that within a common framework of government and law, different ethnic and religious groups can do their own thing. This last is also known as multi-culturalism.

Positivism Into the realm of knowledge with this. Knowledge is also called episteme, but that’s all Greek to most people. Positivism says if you want to know something, use scientific method to get to the truth. There’s also logical or empirical positivism, originated by the Vienna Circle. It stresses science is the path to truth, forget metaphysical approaches say the LPs.

Post-modernism If something comes after the modern era, as in post-modernism, that means we are talking about the future, yes? No, it’s not that in philosophy. Post-modernism refers to a vague method where ideas from different sources are lumped together and then the bones are picked out. Specifically, it’s a reference to different, 20<sup>th</sup> century, philosophical perspectives characterised by jaundiced, analytical views.  Derrida is often touted as a post-modernist, that means you can forget about it.

Pragmatism American philosophers invented pragmatism.  William James said: “What’s true is what works.”  His fellow American, Charles Pierce, mostly went along with this but added that the effects of the apparent truth of statements must be considered. In essence, he said try and find out what is really being communicated, not what you initially think this may be.

Rationalism Reason is king, it’s the source of knowledge, so say the rationalists, for good reason perhaps. Socrates is an early proponent.

Realism In normal parlance something concrete, solid, might be considered real. In philosophical realism this idea of a reality can be extended to non-concrete things. So, Plato’s Perfect Forms, of beauty, justice etc, these are realistic. Things are seen as existing in reality, not just as a concept.  There are several other concepts of realism, follow up if you want to know more.

Representationalism What we see is not the real thing, it’s just representative.

Scepticism We cannot be certain of anything, but can we sure of this? If we are sure, then there is at least one think  we are not sceptical about. Sceptics are closely allied with cynics.

Scholasticism This is where learned mediaevalists attempted to reconcile Christian theology with ancient philosophy, particularly with Aristotle’s sayings.

Scientism It claims that all-natural sciences, as well as the physical sciences, can benefit from the application of scientific method.

Shamanism This is much older than the Abrahamic religions, which may have picked up on some shamanistic beliefs. Shamanism gives us the concept of good and evil, represented by Gods and demons. There are two other key features: firstly, a belief in the existence of ancestral spirits and secondly the conviction that special people, shamans, can access the Gods and spirits for help, through the appropriate rituals. This usually involves the shaman going into a trance-like state, possibly with the help of a drug. Shamanism, like animism goes back to pre-historic times.

Sophism Ancient Greek teachers of philosophy, especially of arête - virtue - and rhetoric, were called sophists.  Protagoras was sophistically inclined. Plato was critical of sophists, and the term came to mean the use of deceptive language.

Solipsism You go on the ultimate ego trip if you believe this one. The only thing that exists is you, your mind, even your body might be a bit dodgy if you don’t think hard enough. See George Berkeley and Rene Descartes.

Stoicism Keep your emotions in check. They can cloud judgement, just take it on the chin. that’s the way of the stoics, plus a bit more. Zeno, he of the uncatchable tortoise, was an early proponent.

Taoism Going for a Chinese here, but chopsticks are not needed. Taoism (sometimes Daoism) is a spiritual, ancient Chinese, philosophy. It says people should seek to live in harmony with the Tao, or Dao, through meditation. The Tao is the base of the whole universe, see Laozi.

Transcendental Idealism Immanuel Kant had this idea that space and time are just something humans perceive. They are not necessarily the real thing.  We make up knowledge of things from our sensory impressions.

Utilitarianism What results in the most good is the most good. Jeremy Bentham came up with this claim. John Stuart Mill rightly amended it.

Chapter 24

Physics and Quantum Mechanics

Classical and Modern Physics: Anyone seriously interested in questions such as: “where did it all begin” and “where will it all end” has to take a hard look at physics. Physics gives us some strong, supported answers. These are not yet perfect and by no means complete, but they give alternative possibilities to Godly scriptures in telling how it was, how it is and how it will be.

In the scientific world physics and its supporting mathematics are crucial in understanding not only the world but also the universe we inhabit. Because of its wide-ranging nature, physics is broken down into several specialist areas. Two of the main disciplines are astro-physics, which is closely linked to cosmology, which looks at the broad picture, and particle physics, which is synonymous with quantum mechanics.

Astro-physics deals with the detail of the very big - the whole universe. It includes galaxies, stars, black holes, planets and the elusive dark energy and dark matter. All this is the stuff of classic physics. This was the original development of physics, which was broad-brush in nature. Classical physics is powerfully underpinned by the theories of Newton and Einstein. Here, Einstein’s theory of General Relativity is the ultimate explanation of the very big, although not the whole story. Since Einstein’s seminal paper we have come to have a much clearer understanding of how the universe works, not just the very big, as expounded by Newton and Einstein, but also the very small. This is the world of minuteness, quantum mechanics.

Quantum mechanics, is part of modern physics.

QM is a tricky subject. In Terry Pratchett’s book, ‘Eric’, the boy Eric asks wizard Rincewind: “What is quantum mechanics?” Rincewind replies: “I don’t know, people who repair quantums I suppose.” Rincewind did not get it quite right. QM is not a job title. QM deals with the very, very small; that is the atom and particles that are far smaller than the atom.

The amazing, ultra-micro universe of sub-atomic particles such as electrons; quarks and neutrinos are increasing revealed by work on QM, which also encompasses these areas:

Interaction between matter, and forces that interact with matter like gravity, the weak and strong nuclear force and the electro-magnetic force;
The concept of motion;
Space-time.

Not unexpectedly, there is some overlap between classical physics and quantum mechanics. For instance, both deal with space-time. Classical physics is concerned with gravity while quantum mechanics speculates about the existence of the graviton, a possible force carrying particle, and gravitational waves, first suggested by physicist and mathematician Oliver Heaviside in 1893. These were finally discovered, disputedly, in 2016. So, the study of physics, especially quantum mechanics, helps us on the road to understanding the entire universe. It may eventually tell us what came before the Big Bang.

Quantum mechanics, what was its origin?
Some of us might think of QM as a very modern science, but its origin goes back to 440 BCE. This is when the Greek Democritus decided to call the smallest possible amount of substance an atom. He did not know it at the time but he had opened up the road of particle physics and fundamental particles. It took about 2,000 years before anyone else drove further down this road. In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell published his theory of electromagnetism; one of the four forces of the Standard Model - more on the SM shortly. British physicist JJ Thompson followed him in 1897. Thompson originated the idea that sub-atomic particles, now known as electrons, were a fundamental component of atoms. He also calculated how tiny they were; about 1,000 times smaller than an atom. Since Thompson’s discovery there has been an explosion of particle discoveries. In the early 1900’s Ernest Rutherford correctly defined the planetary-like structure of the atom. He nearly got it right. Ernest supposed electrons orbiting a central nucleus – like planets orbiting a sun. We know now that electrons don’t orbit. They seem to flicker in and out. Their position is impossible to determine accurately. There’s more on of these four; Democritus, Maxwell, Thompson and Rutherford, and on others later on.

In modern times we realize that the atom of Democritus is not the smallest particle, although his concept of something that cannot be further divided is still relevant. These tinies are now called fundamental particles. ‘Fundamental’ is the qualification used to describe particles, which are not made up of other particles. They are on their own, fundamental in fact. Some fundamentals, quarks and electrons, can be found within an atom.

For example, the simplest atom, hydrogen, comprises of one electron and one proton. The proton is made up of three fundamental particles - quarks. All atoms have electrons and protons. All bar the lightest atom, hydrogen, also have a third negative component, neutrons.  Like their positive neighbour, the proton, these are also made up of three quarks.

In the period between Einstein’s annus mirabilis, 1906,  and the early 1960’s great theoretical physicists teased out the weird properties of life within and outside the atom. From this emerging world of quantum mechanics, more and more fundamental particles were discovered. Some aspects of the quantum mechanics world do not fit neatly with the classical physics defined by Newton and Einstein. This annoyed Einstein no end. He wanted quantum mechanics to show the sort of tidy order that would lead seamlessly into the larger world he had so brilliantly constructed a template for. Newton, the other giant of classical physics, could not be bothered at all, that’s because he was dead long before QM detail appeared on the scene! Einstein was so dismayed at the quantum mechanics he apparently said: “God does not play dice.”

[Figure: 1927 Solvay Conference on Quantum Mechanics, The greatest collection of geniuses in one photo. 17 of those attending became Nobel prize winners. Back row: 6th from left, Erwin Schrodinger; 8th Wolfgang Pauli, 9th Werner Heisenberg. Middle row: 5th from left, Paul Dirac, last, Neils Bohr. Front row: 2nd from left, Max Planck; 3rd Marie Curie; 5th Albert Einstein]

Bizarre Aspects of Quantum Mechanics: Quantum mechanics starts with the simple idea that energy does not come in just any amount; it comes in discrete chunks, called quanta. This is quite easy to understand, but other properties of quantum particles are not at all easy. They are strange and hard to fully comprehend, as even Einstein found. If it weren’t for the fact that they have been tried and tested, these properties would be unbelievable.

Here are those weird quantum properties:

Superposition: A particle exists in all possible states or locations simultaneously, that is, until it is observed. It can be in two places at once; move at different speeds, and have different energy levels. It is only when observed or measured that the particle ‘chooses’ one particular state. Just looking at it makes it decide a single position. There’s the example of Schrodinger’s cat, both alive and dead in its box until the box is opened, then a choice is made and it settles into one or other state. The ‘particles’ referred to in superposition, Schrodinger’s moggy aside, are extremely tiny. The biggest to be scientifically superimposed, as at 2019, had only 356 atoms, so you’ll need a powerful electron microscope to see them.
Entanglement: Two particles can become entangled so that their properties depend on each other - no matter how far apart they get. A measurement of one seems to affect the measurement of the other instantaneously, that is faster than the speed of light - an idea Einstein called "spooky action at a distance". There’s a theory, as yet unproven, that Robins use entangled particles in their retina, together with the Earth’s magnetic field, to navigate. Each year, in Autumn, they fly from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean, without any use of maps!
Tunnelling: A particle can push through an energy barrier, it disappears on one side of it and emerges on the other. It’s just like walking straight through a wall without knocking it down. Recent developments in quantum biology have looked at how the quantum world is important to life. Enzymes, essential to life, use the quantum tunnelling magic to transfer electrons and protons from one molecule to another, so speeding up the chemical reaction in a living cell. This was discovered in the 1970’s and 1980’s.

The above are definite, proven quantum effects, apart from the Robin. There are two more speculative, and even weirder possible quantum associations: retro-causality and the multiverse. First, retro-causality:

What’s to come effects what’s past and what’s now
Retro-causality

[Figure: Diagram: a triangle of double-headed arrows linking three boxes, "Present" (green, top), "Future" (blue, bottom left) and "Past" (red, bottom right)]

Retro-causality is also known as reverse causality. It proposes that there can be a reverse of cause and effect.

Retro-causality says you can have something happen before its cause, so the future can impact on the past. The theory suggests particles like positrons could move backwards in time, as an electron, which then gains a positive charge. When the positron meets an electron, which has a negative charge, they annihilate each other. This annihilation is an event happening before the cause – the time travelling positron. Speculatively – there is not an ounce of supporting evidence – forms of retro-causality might allow traversable wormholes, so that we humans could enjoy time-travel. Retro-causality may also have some, as yet unknown, association with the proven effect of quantum entanglement. This could help explain a great deal of the seeming magic of the quantum world. It gives a new slant on the nature of reality.

Some of this magic of the quantum world is very useful in modern applications: computers; tablets; smart phones and imaging. Quantum effects may also be very relevant in biology. In their 2014 book “Life on the Edge” physicist Jim Al-Khalili and molecular geneticist Johnjoe McFadden argue that the quantum effect can be found in animal cells. This follows on the work of Erwin Schrödinger some 70 years earlier. He made a case for a link between quantum physics and biology. In Jim and Johnjoe’s book they cite the example of the European Robin and how it is able to navigate on its migratory route to the south using quantum entanglement.

[Figure: Photographs of Jim Al-Khalili and Johnjoe McFadden, captioned "Jim Al-Khalili" and "Johnjoe McFadden"]

There’s the well-known double slit experiment, this demonstrates one more quantum effect. Single electrons, which are fired at the two slits, go through both at the same time. The experiment illustrates that quantum particles can be both a particle and a wave. As a wave they can go through both but not as separate particles. This quantum property is called wave-particle duality.

If quantum effects are so common - we know of some used in electronics, which is everywhere - why can’t we humans use all their features? It would be so useful to be able to walk through walls, using quantum tunnelling. This ability would save on the cost of doors. It would also make life more interesting for those responsible for bank vault security. Being able to be in two places at once would be quite handy too. We could navigate without the need for GPS devices, and watch a rugby match while at the same time sitting down at home to catch up on that episode of Downton Abbey or Doctor Who that we missed.

If we weren’t sure which of two doors to go through, the ability to pass through both at the same time, acting like a wave, would save messing about.

Sadly, we cannot use this quantum magic, at least not yet. This is because the quantum effect seems to work very well with minute particles but progressively diminishes, as they get larger. Perhaps if we dieted extremely rigourously……..?

A multiverse? Arguably the strangest and most exciting aspect of quantum mechanics is that it may point to the existence of a multiverse. The multiverse assumes there are an infinitive number of universes, other than our own. In which case anything that can happen will have happened in one universe or other. There are several versions of this theory, none have any supporting proof but the idea seems to be gaining in popularity. The continuing debate, about whether the multiverse does or does not exist, has divided the physics and cosmological community. Those in favour include: Stephen Hawking, Brian Greene, Max Tegmark, Michio Kaku, Martin Rees, Laura Mersini-Houghton, and Sean Carroll. Among the opponents are: David Gross, Paul Steinhardt, Neil Turok, Viatcheslav Mukhanov, Michael S. Turner and Roger Penrose.

Parallel universes Closely allied to the more usual concept of the ‘multiverse’ are ‘parallel universes’. These are said to mimic our own universe except for variation caused by an event, which could be large or small. For example, in a parallel universe Hitler and the Nazis could have won the second World War. That’s a big event. Another parallel universe might diverge because a person went to work on a bike whereas in our universe that same person had caught a bus. US physicist Hugh Everett is seen as the father of parallel universes theory, called the many-worlds theory. He came up with this idea in the nineteen fifties. There is absolutely no evidence at all for parallel universes, but it remains a potent idea with physicists in modern times. The ‘many-worlds’ idea though remains unproven, pure speculation.

In his BBC radio interview by Jim Al Khalili, Martin Rees explained the idea of a multiverse. He said there could be many Big Bangs resulting in different universes with very different physical laws to ours, but he accepts this is a long way from being proven. It could be reasoned that if conditions existed some 13.8 billion years ago, that gave rise to the singularity and Big Bang, why couldn’t the same conditions result in more Big Bangs, and many universes? If it’s a monotheistic God who kicked off everything, why would He stop at creating just the one universe - boring?

Many universes

Nobel prize winner Steven Weinberg said in 2007 that if the multiverse existed then we could never fully tease out all of the Standard Model reasoning : "..the hope of finding a rational explanation for the precise values of quark masses and other constants of the Standard Model that we observe in our Big Bang is doomed, for their values would be an accident of the particular part of the multiverse in which we live." These other universes would have different basic physics to our own. In many the electro-magnetic force would not exist. Therefore, atoms could not be formed and so neither could stars or planets.” The multiverse remains an exciting speculation. Sadly, at present, it’s only in Science Fiction that we can move between universes. Now back to those fundamental particles.

Standard Model This theory attempts to impose a structure on fundamental particles, and to some very small extent tame quantum mechanics. It is also the best yet proven attempt to come with a theory that draws together classic Newtonian/Einsteinian physics with the bizarre world of quantum mechanics.

The Standard Model proposes that there are 12 fundamental particles of all matter and that these are acted on by one of more of four force carrying particles.

Quarks (purple): up (u) 2/3, 1/2; charm (c) 2/3, 1/2; top (t) 2/3, 1/2; down (d) ≈4.8 MeV/c², -1/3, 1/2; strange (s) ≈95 MeV/c², -1/3, 1/2; bottom (b) ≈4.18 GeV/c², -1/3, 1/2.
