Chapter 25

The Universe, history, size and content

Back then, 13.8 billion years ago, it was a singular beginning, in both senses. The singularity that went bang was odd, in the extreme, that sort of singular. We are not sure whether it was the only one, so no claim to this dictionary version of singular. And, as the original, cosmological meaning, the singularity was so dense it's well short of the mark to call it thick. It did, though, very quickly become as thick as a plank, becoming quite a few light years thick in super-quick Planck time.

Planck Epoch

The very, very early universe is known as the Planck Epoch, after the German, Max Planck with his genius at working out impossible numbers. He calculated a time of 10<sup>-43</sup> seconds after the Big Bang during which the laws of physics did not yet apply. That time is 0.0 of a second with another 42 '0s' before 1. Stuff was still sorting itself out during this miniscule time and, it's thought, the four fundamental forces were combined into one. Luckily for us, the universe did begin to sort itself out. The laws of physics cranked into life. Fundamental particles, full of community spirit, started happily joining up to form those first atoms of hydrogen, then helium. Atoms started bumping into each other, and with the help of a weak gravitational force, began to clump together into larger and larger masses. It took about 100 million years for this process to result in the first stars. Early stars got together to create the first galaxy, 200 million years after the BB.

Some original particles, swarming around just after the BB, were aggressive and not at all community minded. These, when meeting similarly bolshy anti-matter particles, wiped each other out in their own mini Big Bang. But there were enough kind and reasonable particles left to allow our universe to grow.

Cosmic Microwave Background

This ancient radiation has, amazingly been detected. It is a leftover of the Big Bang, originating about 380,000 years after the beginning of our Universe, that's more than 13 billion years ago. Here it is, the Universe long before us, before dinosaurs, before Earth, the Sun and even before the Milky Way:

[Figure: Oval map of the cosmic microwave background, speckled blue, green and yellow]

headings.text: The Universe, history, size and content

pages.text:
In 1964 two radio astronomers, Robert Wilson and Arno Penzias came across some continous noise in a huge microwave receiver. This proved to be the evidence of our early Universe, the Cosmic Microwave Background. Both were recognised with the Nobel Prize for this breakthrough in our understanding of the Universe's origin. Some fifty years later, the European Space Agency's Planck mission probe collected light in very fine detail. This allowed the CMB map to be made.

And in the End

We have a great deal of evidence to suggest how the universe began and developed, but we know much less about how it might end. The type of ending and its timing is uncertain. It's so uncertain as to be not in any way certain, Physicists and astronomers give very broad ball park figures of the time to the end, anywhere between 5 billion to 1 trillion years from now. The manner of demise is also not known. Guesses include: the big freeze - all energy is used up; big rip - everything is pulled asunder; big crunch - everything collapses; cosmic bounce - allied to the big crunch. This says after the crunch there will be another Big Bang = a reoccurring universe.

[Figure: Our universe - What Happens in the end?]

That's what is guessed about the universe's eventual demise, now more about its beginning.

Supernova

Those early atoms, hydrogen and helium, were a bit light on mass, but en-masse in stars they got very hot. There were some very big stars in the early universe who did not last too long. Forces of gravity eventually overcame the very gradually cooling star as it ran out of fuel. The star's weakening propellent force and pressure from nuclear energy, pushing outwards, was vanquished by gravity. In an almighty collapse some giant stars crushed so violently and quickly - in just a few seconds - they exploded. This was a supernova.

Supernova, the Key to Life

[Figure: What holds a star together? Courtesy of NASA]

These, the biggest explosive events in our universe, were vital to the eventual formation of life. The immense pressures and incredible heat generated, reaching billions of degrees kelvin, was transformational on the atom front. Many of those simple atoms of hydrogen and helium in the exploding star had their electrons and nuclei knocked about a lot, first by the enormous pressures created by gravity then by the explosive force and heat. Hydrogen and helium re-formed into new configurations of heavier atoms. Supernova gave birth to these heavier, more complex atoms of carbon, oxygen and iron, among others. Some of these make up human bodies, plants, animals and Earth itself. We Modern Humans need carbon and oxygen. Our bodies have 18% is of the former with a huge 65% of oxygen. Iron is included in a small, but vital quantity. There's about 4 grams of iron in adults.

Supernova, ergo, are essential to all life and have been a feature of our universe throughout nearly all of its history. On average, in our Milky Way galaxy, there's one supernova every 100 years.

[Figure: Cassiopeia A, a supernova 11,000 light years away and 10 light years wide.]

Giant Early Stars

The very earliest stars were super-massive; known as Population 111 stars.  Their size meant they were more unstable than most of today's stars, who are much smaller. Small is a relative term in respect of stars. Our Sun is an average size star at 864,000 miles in diameter, more than 100 times the diameter of Earth. On this comparison our Sun seems huge, but it's quite minuscule compared to the early stars, some P3 were more akin to Betelgeuse in size, big B is 600 million miles in diameter. P3's could be even bigger than B.

The early, giant stars did not last long, sometimes just a few hundred thousand years, maybe up to a few million years.

When they exploded, in a supernova, they spewed out the vital heavier elements. Meteors, asteroids and planets picked up these essential elements. All this eventually led to Modern Humans, us. Thank you, supernova.

How Big is the Universe?

This universe of ours is mightily big. Some people will say: "Ah, I can work out the size of the universe because I know its age and that man Einstein said nothing can travel faster than the speed of light, so its diameter has to be 2 x 13.8 billion light years = 27.4 billion light years." This is an understandable calculation, but wrong. To the edge of the observable universe is about 46.5 billion light years, or it's 93 billion light years in diameter. Expansion of the fabric of space is the reason for this. Space expansion is not governed by the limitation of the speed of light, this rules how fast matter can move. Space simply says "No matter, I'm going to ignore Einstein's speed limitation." Expansion means that the universe is continually getting bigger. By the time you read this it might be an extra 0.1 billion light years larger, or more.

Expanding Universe

[Figure: Black and white portrait of Edwin Hubble with a pipe, arms folded over a cat]

We have that great American astronomer, cat lover, Cambridge University student, and Nobel Prize winner Edwin Hubble to thank for the proof that the universe is expanding. In 1924 he used the 100-inch telescope on Mount Wilson to measure the distance of galaxies. Edwin identified certain stable stars that could be used as a sort of base line, called standard candles, or Cepheid variables (originally discovered by a woman astronomer, Henrietta Swan Leavitt). Not only did he find that our universe was expanding but that the further away a galaxy was, the faster it is receding - Hubble's Law.

The work of Hubble blew out of the water Einstein's 'steady state' theory of the universe. Albert's brilliant early equations would not give him the 'steady state' theory he was wedded too. To make steady state work he had to shove in a made-up factor, the Cosmological Constant, an imagined repulsive force, in one of his field equations of General Relativity. Albert honestly later admitted the Cosmological Constant was his biggest mistake.

This is Einstein's not quite so famous equation - the dodgy 'fix' he used to get to an unmoving universe: R<sub>μν</sub> − Rg<sub>μν</sub> = <sub>2</sub> T<sub>μν</sub>,

If translated into a football match score, Hubble's expansion team versus Einstein's steady state eleven, the result would be a walk-over, say 10 for Hubble and 0 for Einstein. Albert may have lost out on this one but he was a great winner in other areas, relatively speaking.

Back again to Hubble. He generally gets most of the plaudits re the expanding universe theory, but two before him deserve serious mention, George Lemaitre, and the interestingly named Vesto Slipher. George was a Belgian Catholic priest. He was also a mathematician with a keen interest in astronomy, and like Edwin, went to Cambridge University.

[Figure: The Large Magellanic Cloud. Taken by the Hubble space telescope 2020, on the 30th anniversary of its time in space. Image: NASA, ESA, STScI]

Two years before Hubble's 1924 breakthrough, George identified an expanding universe, but his work was not as widely publicised or accepted as Hubble's. George also came up with another remarkable, and now established idea, that of the universe's origin, the Big Bang. He really should have been a shoe-in for a Nobel Prize. Sadly, he proved that while ground-breaking scientific work is important, so is publicity and recognition, which he never sufficiently received. In acknowledgment of his work, Hubble's Law is now commonly, and rightly, referred to as Hubble-Lemaitre Law.

[Figure: Black and white photograph of George Lemaitre in clerical dress with medals]

[Figure: Black and white photograph of Vesto Slipher in a suit and tie]

Now for Vesto Slipher, no, his first name is not a mis-spelt box of matches (Vesta). He was an American astronomer, who did not go to Cambridge University. He was working about ten years before Hubble. Vesto discovered distant galaxies were 'redshifted'. Redshift is nothing to do with ladies' underwear. It means viewing the light wavelength, some move quicker or slower than others, to indicate galactic standstill, recession or growth.

In this case the redshift indicated galaxies receding from us. Hubble's work was more detailed, and his arguments backed up with lots of solid evidence. It helped that the Mount Wilson telescope was the largest in the world at the time. Observations made with it were convincing. His papers were therefore widely read and accepted by the scientific community, so he still retains the top-man status in bringing the expansion theory to prominence. Slipher slipped away from public renown.

What's beyond the Universe?

Our universe started from nothing so it's everything there is. Just like the surface of a balloon it has no edges. There's also no middle. In this sense it is not expanding into anything. Supreme astrophysicist Stephen Hawking said that there is no outside to the universe, asking what's beyond the universe is like asking what is north of the North Pole. Yes, but what is north of the North Pole?

Universe Size in Parsecs and Astronomical Units

Now we can understand why the universe is so much bigger than might be expected. Coming back to its size, if you want to calculate that 46.5 billion light years in another way, try counting it in parsecs. These are 3.26 light years each. This makes the radius of our universe about 14.3 billion parsecs. Parsecs are calculated based on 1 astronomical unit and the distance from the intersection of 1 arcsecond angle. Light years are easier to comprehend!

In terms of astronomic units - one of these is the distance from Earth to the Sun - we have a much bigger number: There are 63,241 AU in a light year, so 46 billion times 63,241 is?? We won't bother to try and calculate in miles or kilometres. There are just not enough numbers, well there are, but unpowered it would take up too many lines.

Size and Type of Stars

We've seen something about the size of the universe, who's top when it comes to stars? At the moment a super-red giant star with an unmemorable name, UY Scuti, is in first place. This monster is much bigger than mighty Betelgeuse; almost 2.5 times.

[Figure: Diagram of the Sun as a tiny dot beside the huge orange disc of UY Scuti, labelled "Sun" and "UY Scuti"]

To put it in a solar system perspective, UY Scuti is 1,700 times larger than our Sun. It's a long way from us, at 5,219 light years, with intervening stars and dust. This is why we don't easily see it.

headings.text: Universe Size in Parsecs and Astronomical Units

pages.text:
Brown Dwarf, the in betweener These objects are too big to be classified as planets. They form in the same way as stars, through collapsing gas and dust clouds, but don't become dense enough for fusion to start, as it does with a star. They are a sort of failed star. If they had a bit more mass they would become Red Dwarf Stars.

Black Holes

Black Holes are the greediest, most omnivorous entities in the entire universe. They will eat any and everything, even light. The photons of light travel so fast they can reach our moon from Earth in one second, but light is not fast enough to get away from a Black Hole, if it gets too close. These supreme gobblers exercise incredibly powerful gravitational muscle to draw in their prey - gas, space dust, planets and even stars. Once inside their maw Black Holes crush their victims down to a tiny fraction of their previous size.

[Figure: Gigantic Black Hole at the centre of Messier 87 galaxy. It contains the mass of 6.5 billion Suns. M87 is a super-giant galaxy 54 million light years away.]

The Event Horizon Telescope project came up with this, the first clear image of a Black Hole. The project was an amazing collaboration. It brought together 200 scientists in observatories around the world. These observatories combined and synchronised in such a way that to produce a telescope the size of planet Earth. It collected an enormous amount of data about galaxy M87, this took 2 years to analyse and produce the picture above. M87 has an enormous Black Hole, but this is by no means the biggest. The largest discovered, as at 2019, is in the galaxy cluster, Abell 85. It is 40 billion times our Sun's mass and 700 million light years from Earth.

Very big Black Holes are the Kings of the cosmos. They sit in the centre of their galaxies. Galactic stars and planets swirl respectfully around them.

What else about Black Holes? Well, as the name 'Event Horizon Telescope' suggests, All Black Holes have an Event Horizon. This is the boundary around a Black Hole beyond which nothing can escape it, not even light. It's the point from which nothing can return because the gravitational pull of the Black Hole is too strong. Black Holes spin at close to the speed of light so stuff is both drawn in and around them.

Wormholes

A favourite of science fiction, these are a predicted by Einstein's General Relativity theory. They are claimed to be bridges, Einstein - Rosen bridges, across space-time. They are like tunnels, from one place to another. If they work and we could find how to use them, it could mean a form of speedy short cut over vast distances in the universe. Wormholes remain speculative.

How Many Galaxies and Stars?

Among many things about our universe that's hard to imagine and understand is how could there be an object incredibly tiny in size, far smaller than the smallest atom, have enough matter and energy to produce the current universe? This 'singularity' has resulted in today's 2 trillion galaxies, with maybe 100 billion stars or more in each - exact numbers are not known. Cosmologists say that on average there are 3 or more exoplanets around every star. That means we need a big sheet of paper to write down in full, unpowered arithmetic, the possible number of planets in the universe.

[Figure: A beautiful image by Hubble of the Sombrero galaxy, 50,000 light-years across and 28 million light years from Earth. It has 800 billion stars.]

Nebulae

These are the most gigantic factories in the cosmos. They churn out stars, acting both as a birthplace and nursery. Well, the churning is to a cosmic timescale and very slow in human terms. Nebulae are enormous clouds of interstellar dust and gas, hydrogen mostly. They can be millions of light years across. Sometimes, they're formed by the material spewed out from a supernova. The death of one star can lead to the birth of another, eventually. The process can take several hundred million years. In nebulae atoms begin clumping together. The force of gravity results in bigger and bigger clumps. It's mostly all hydrogen at first, when the accumulated mass recaches a critical stage it collapses and this starts a nuclear reaction - a star is born.

[Figure: The Pillars Of Creation, 4+ light years wide. Part of the Eagle Nebula]

If the mass is insufficient to cause a nuclear reaction, a planet emerges. Nebulae give birth to big babies, stars, or small babies, planets.

What about Exoplanets?

Unlike the estimated total number of alien planets, which is assumed to be at least 3 for every star, there are exoplanets which have been firmly discovered. These are planets that have been observed to orbit stars other than our local Sun. The number found rises constantly. By October 2020 nearly 4,300 exoplanets had been found. Most of these were revealed by the Kepler space telescope. The biggest discovered by June 2020 is Kepler 88d. This is 6 times more massive than Jupiter. It obviously has plenty of space but there would still be an almighty crush. Of course, many exoplanets, just like most planets in the solar system, are not conducive to supporting life, or as we know it, carbon-based life. But given the gigantic number of exoplanets, some will have conditions with some similarity to Earth. Some discoveries possibly have water. and it is by no means certain that all life must be carbon based. Statistically, it seems unlikely that planet Earth has the only intelligent life in the universe, so the question is..........

Are we Alone?

Are we, MH, the only intelligent life in the universe? We don't know for sure. No aliens have made their presence unambiguously known on earth. The SETI project, which has been running for 50 years, has not yet made contact. However, short of this type of certainty we now know a lot more about exoplanets and the construction of the universe. These new findings throw up some indicative numbers which give statistical weight to a "no" we are not alone answer.

[Figure: E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial film poster: E.T. and three children in front of a large moon. Maybe ET is not just a film?]

NASA's Kepler mission reveals that about 17% of stars have Earth like planets orbiting them. That means upwards of 17 billion such planets in the Milky Way, our own galaxy. And as there are estimated to be 2 trillion galaxies, there will be many trillions of rocky, i.e. Earth like planets, in the universe

Even if only one in a million of these rocky planets has water and other minerals conducive to life, there will be many millions of planets like Earth. So, it's reasonable to assume intelligent life has evolved on many planets in the universe.

And some of these alien intelligences have had time to become much more advanced than us. On older star systems in some galaxies Earth like planets could be 2 to 3 billion years older than Earth. One more thought about the possibility of discovering alien life. Since light takes so long to reach us we are always looking back a long way in time. Aside from a limited number of stars local to the Sun, light reaching us is from several hundred up to several billions of years ago. Advanced, detectable, alien civilisations may not have had time to develop. They could be there now, but we cannot detect 'now' because when we look up at the stars, we only see the past.

The Hubble Space Telescope, among several, is probably best known. It overlapped with Kepler. Next up for NASA, plus other partners, is the James Webb Space Telescope, due to be launched in 2021 by an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana.

[Figure: James Webb Telescope, It will explore in the infrared with a 6.5 metre primary mirror. Webb is a collaboration between NASA, the European Space Agency and the Canadian Space Agency.]

It is known as a 'Next Generation Space Telescope (NGST)'; meaning it has the very latest, more sensitive, technology, and will be able to probe deeper and more fully than its predecessors, Kepler, Hubble and Spitzer.'

Excitingly it will seek out potentially habitable exoplanets, especially looking at the Trappist-1 system, this is 40 light years from Earth, with 3 exoplanets. Apart from looking for possible life bearing exoplanets Webb will also study every stage of the history of our Universe. It had better find something of great interest, having cost 10 billion dollars.

While Webb is definitely on the go, NASA has other more hopeful plans. One is for a similar Hubble type, infrared scope, named 'Luvoir' for Large Ultraviolet Optical Infrared Surveyor. Luvoir would have 6 times the resolution of Hubble. Potential costs are enormous so Luvoir remains partly a dream as at June 2020 with a proposed launch date of 2039..

Comets, Asteroids and Meteors

For life to get going on our planet, or exoplanets, comets are essential early on, because they deliver water. Later, they are not wanted because their impact can cause extinctions. These icy, gassy tailed, lumps of rock and can be over 10 kilometres in size. Comets are fragments left over from when solar systems first formed. They can occasionally be drawn in by a planet's gravity and cause devastation on impact.

Asteroids are similar but are of airless rock. They don't have gassy tails. Meteors are very small, often they are bits of asteroids or comets that have broken off entering our atmosphere. They burn up in fiery streaks sometimes called shooting stars.

Solar System - Some Facts

Our home planet Earth is the third from the Sun, at an average of 93 million miles distance, or one Astronomical Unit.

The full planetary line up is: little Mercury (about a third of Earth in size), just 36 million miles from the Sun, then Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and finally, at 2.8 billion miles from the Sun we have Neptune. Pluto was also included until 2006 when it was relegated to dwarf planet status. Planets do not orbit in perfect circles. Orbits are elliptical so distances from the sSun vary , for instance max distance for Earth is 94.5 million miles, on aphelion day in July. Its January minimum, the perihelion, is 91.3 million miles. Light can take 4 hours 9 minutes to reach Neptune, furthest planet, compared to 8.3 minutes to get to Earth.

The solar system's 4 rocky planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, with more gas than rock. The final 2, Uranus and Neptune, are known as ice giants. Giant really is an appropriate adjective. Compared to Earth, the smallest giant, Neptune, is 58 times bigger in size and 17 times as massive. The biggest, mighty Jupiter, is 1,321 times bigger, although lower density means it's just 318 times as massive. If you ever manage to travel to Neptune, take a very warm coat. The temperature is minus 200 Celsius, but no worries about gravity. You will only feel 14% heavier. Not good for those on a diet

[Figure: Kuiper Belt, Credit ESA, Oort Cloud (The outer ring)]

The solar system size is defined by the Oort Cloud. This is like a giant shell completely surrounding space beyond the planets. It's between 0.3 to 3 light years from the Sun. The Oort Cloud has a huge number of orbiting rock particles and is the home of long-period comets, i.e. those that take more than 200 years to orbit the Sun. Closer to the Sun is the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy material, including short-period comets. It is similar to the asteroid belt but much larger, at 2.8 billion to 4.6 billion miles from the Sun. The asteroid belt, with its millions of asteroids, is in a torus shaped orbit between Mars and Jupiter. Most planets have attendant moons. Saturn has the most at 82. Some moons of Jupiter and Saturn, like Europa, Titan, Enceladus, Ganymede and Callisto, may have water and could support life.

The Milky Way and its Neighbourhood

Our solar system resides in the Milky Way, a big galaxy some 100 thousand light years across.

[Figure: An actual image of the Milky Way taken by the COBE satellite, DIRBE (Diffuse Infrared Background Experiment), NASA]

Our solar system sits in a spiral arm called the Orion Arm, about 20,000 light years from the centre. The Voyager spacecraft travels at some 10 miles each second. It could go around the entire Earth in less than 1 hour, that seems fast, but it would take Voyager 450 million years to reach the MW centre.

We serenely orbit the centre, well if you call moving at close to 500,000 miles an hour serene. But we don't notice the movement. There's not even a sign of a strong wind. Our solar system speed in the Orion Arm is sufficient to twirl us around the MW in just 250 million years. Cosmic numbers are big.

headings.text: The Milky Way and its Neighbourhood

pages.text:
A for Andromeda

Our mighty galactic neighbour, the Andromeda Galaxy, is 2.5 million light years away and 260,000 light years across. With a top estimate of 1 trillion stars it's over three times the Milky Way's 300 billion or so, Andromeda is due to crash into the Milky Way in 4.5 billion years. Given the size of the gaps between stars it won't be much of a crash. Those Andromeda stars who have been well brought up will be saying to a new MW neighbour: "I'm so sorry, is this your orbital path? I could not help coming in this direction. Dark Matter and Dark Energy gave me a shove. I just couldn't see what they were up to."

Andromeda is our neighbouring galaxy but the nearest star to the solar system is Proxima Centauri, one of the Alpha Centauri binary stars. If we could travel at the speed of light it would take us 4.2 years to get there.

[Figure: Andromeda, the Milky Way's neighbour who will drop in on us one day]

Monster Galaxy Godzilla

Thanks to NASA's space telescope, Hubble, the biggest local galaxy yet known, in terms of size, is the Godzilla galaxy. At 463,000 light years across, it's bigger than Andromeda and 4.6 times the size of our own, Milky Way galaxy. The MW is recognised as a large galaxy but Godzilla dwarfs it. Godzilla has a super-massive black hole at its centre, 1 trillion stars and is 232 million light years away in the northern constellation of Perseus.

Quasars

They are extremely energetic and extremely long towers of particles streaming out from the poles of some Black Holes at almost the speed of light. Quasars derive from the 'accretion disc' of material around a super massive Black Hole. Their energy is so great, it can be trillions of volts. It outshines the entire galaxy they are located in. Quasars brightness can be between 10 to 100,000 times that of the entire Milky Way galaxy.

They are not only supremely bright they also extend a very long way. Material from a quasar can project one million light years. Planets containing life have to stay clear of these quasar jets, otherwise kaput.

Fortunately, our own Earth is not in any quasar's sights, mainly because quasars are relatively rare, that's because they require super-massive Black Holes to power them.

Pulsars

These are not so powerful as quasars. Pulsars send out pulses of light from a very small but extremely dense Neutron star.

Neutron stars have a mighty magnetic field, which gives them their pulse power. They are about the size of a large city, but have more mass than our Sun. Radiation pulses arise because of the star's rapid rotation, commonly one per second. The super quicks spin at more than 200 times a second.

[Figure: Artist impression of a Quasar, hopefully at least a billion light years from Earth]

[Figure: Pulsar, courtesy of NASA]

Dark Matter and Dark Energy

What's the Universe made of? This is it:

68% dark energy, equivalent to Einstein's cosmological constant,
27% dark matter,
4.9% normal the stuff of stars, planets, asteroids, dust etc, i.e. protons, neutrons and electrons,
0.1% neutrinos and antineutrinos,
about 0.008% photons.

This breakdown means that we don't see most of it. Nor can we detect, yet, the 95% represented by dark matter and dark energy. These are just theoretical things, which must be there because something is operating against gravitational forces to produce space expansion. Dark matter and dark energy have yet to be confidently discovered.

[Figure: Pie chart: Dark matter, Dark energy, and a thin yellow slice labelled "The matter we understand. All the planets, comets, stars, galaxies, black holes, and more." Dark Matter, NASA Space Place]

And Before the Big Bang?

Yes, we know, or think we do, that our Universe started with the Big Bang, that immensely dense singularity that blew up, balloon like. What came before the Big Bang? The BB arose from an incredibly tiny particle which can be seen as a seed of a new Universe or as some would say, a God Particle. But what created this seed? One idea has been put forward by Polish physicist Dr. Nikodem Poplawski. He suggests that in a Black Hole, of super-super size, compacting material is stopped by the BH spin. Black Holes can spin close to the speed light.  This creates an enormous torsional effect on the super-compacted material. It becomes not only super heavy but also violently twisted. The twisting can suddenly release in the form of a Big Bang, or big bounce as Dr Poplawski prefers to say. Thus, we have a new Universe. Black Holes are a one-way door between two Universes, claims Dr Poplawski. Now, given there are billions of Black Holes, with each one likely to pop out a new Universe, this idea might also add credence to the Multiverse concept.

[Figure: Diagram: a black blob labelled "Hyper Black Hole 13.82 Billion years ago" with an arrow to a yellow box labelled "The Universe ?"]

What of God?

The Abrahamic religions claim creation of our universe was not by a Black Hole, but by God. As we've already seen, there is no proof of this, but likewise nor is there proof of the Black Hole progenitor idea. Over many centuries, scientific understanding of our Universe has increased. We've moved on a long way since our hunter-gatherer forbearers may have thought stars were deceased ancestors (see Noth's story Chapter 5), and from Aristotle and the Catholic church's belief that the Earth was at the centre of it all.

In the early 20<sup>th</sup> century, the Milky Way galaxy was thought to be the entire Universe, and that our Universe was static, unchanging. We now know there are billions of other galaxies and that the Universe is not static at all, it's expanding with increasing rapidity.

Cosmologists and astrophysicists are continuing to discover and understand more. Eventually we may be able to come up with an answer to Universal origin, the Great Theory of Everything, and be able to prove it. Meanwhile, it's hard for us to contemplate the origin of all, i.e., what it is that comes from nothing. Is it possible for there to be nothing? In pondering this question we should 'bear' in mind what Winnie the Pooh said about 'nothing':

[Figure: Winnie the Pooh cartoon with raised arms]

People say doing nothing is impossible but I do nothing every day.

Winnie the Pooh

chapters.title: Humans see the Past and Travel so Fast
chapters.summary: Pub quiz questions - humans - how long have they existed, how fast do they travel, can they time travel? Here are the answers!

pages.text:
Chapter 26

Humans see the Past and Travel so Fast

Some good pub quiz questions could be these:

How long have humans been in the Universe?
Can humans go back in time?
What is the fastest speed that any human has travelled?
For a bonus point, have any bits of us moved faster than answer to 3? 3

All the answers are below.

We were there at The Beginning (almost!) and will be there at The End

Our universe cannot be avoided. It's all around us. We are a part of it. An infinitesimal, tiny fragment, but still a part, and we will always be a part of it. In fact, we've been in this universe of ours almost since its beginning, 13.8 billion years ago. Shortly after the kick-off - that Big Bang - atoms began to be formed. The first atoms were of hydrogen, appearing about 380,000 years after the BB. Our bodies are made up of atoms, molecules and their basic components - electrons and quarks. As previously noted, the great Carl Sagan said "We are star stuff." These fundamental particles of ours are pretty ancient and will go on for a long, long time after our demise. The particles that make up our bodies are as old as 99.99% of the universe's age. We will be there at the end, nearly, but in an unconscious, unstructured, very bitty form.

Looking up at the Time Machine

[Figure: Calendar with a clock]

An interesting point to note, among many, is that when we look out at the night sky with our eyes, binoculars or telescopes we are always looking back in time. The nearest star to our solar system, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 billion light years away.  That means we see it as it was just over 4 years ago. Distant galaxies, spied with the mighty Hubble space telescope, are many billions of light years away. The light we see from some galaxies originated before planet Earth was formed, 4.6 billion years ago. This feature gives rise to another cosmological term, the Cosmic Event Horizon named for the edge of the universe. Any light emitted today from the CEH can never reach us, because the space in between is moving away faster than the speed of light. The Cosmic Event Horizon is 16 billion light years away.

headings.text: Humans see the Past and Travel so Fast
We were there at The Beginning (almost!) and will be there at The End
Looking up at the Time Machine

pages.text:
Eventually, all galaxies and stars beyond the CEH won't be seen. There will just be black, empty looking space. Of course, by the time this happens humans probably won't be around to see it, or rather not see it

So Still yet so Fast and so Far

Perception is not truth. It is all in the eye of the beholder and what is commonly accepted. (see philosophers Xenophanes, Bishop Berkeley, and Michel Foucault).

We think that we can be sure about something, but that depends on the angle from which we are looking. Apparent certainties can be just that - apparent. For instance, when someone has a good night's sleep, say sleeping for 8 hours that person might say that they had not moved any distance in the night. But the Earth revolves completely once every 24 hours. Meaning Earth is turning on its axis at a rate of just over 1,000 miles an hour.

The Earth is not only turning on its axis. It also orbits our Sun. Earth orbits the Sun in 1 year, covering 150 million miles at a speed of 67,000 miles an hour. The Sun is moving in relation to the Milky Way galaxy, dragging Earth and other solar system planets with it at a respectable 486,000 miles an hour. Lastly, our Milky Way galaxy itself is moving through the universe, along with its 200 billion stars, including the Sun and planet Earth. Our galaxy moves through space at a rate of 1,342,000 miles an hour.

[Figure: Cartoon of a man asleep in a bed, "zzzzz"]

The sleeper, is unaware that he's moved in a number of directions, at different speeds, during his 8 hours sleep.

To recap:

Our sleeper has rotated with the Earth at a measly 1,000 miles an hour, shifting position some 8,000 miles;The Earth speeds around the Sun at 67,000 miles an hour. He's moved with it; a distance of 536,000 miles;
Our Sun races around its home galaxy at 486,000 mph. Now our sleeper has moved 3,888,000 miles;
The Sun itself is hauled along with the Milky Way's part in universal expansion. In 8 hours, with our sleeper on board, moving at 1.3 million mph, it has travelled 10,736,000 miles.

So, during his night's good sleep our slumberer has travelled a maximum distance equivalent to taking 20 return trips to the moon and back.

headings.text: So Still yet so Fast and so Far

pages.text:
But he thinks he hasn't moved all night, apart from turning over occasionally, or going to the loo perhaps. Quite a moving story don't you think?

Finally, on speed, bits of us, that is tiny, non-sentient, fundamental particles have moved fastest of all. These have speeded along at near the speed of light when they were originally ejected from a supernova - we are star stuff remember.

Some very moving images:

[Figure: Globe showing the Americas with the axis of rotation and a rotation arrow]

Planet Earth and all its inhabitants rotate on its axis at over 1,000 mph

Something very big smacked into the Earth a long time ago. This caused Earth's axis to tilt about 24° in relation to the sun, giving us the seasons.

The Earth, and us, orbit the Sun in 365 and a bit days at 67,000 mph

[Figure: Diagram of the Earth at four points in its orbit around the Sun]

The Milky Way spiral galaxy speeds through space at 1.3 million mph, this is the fastest speed any and complete humans have travelled at. It's continually speeding up, because of the universe's expansion.

Expansion of space - impact on what can be seen from Earth

The Sun and its attendant planets, Earth included, spins in the Orion spiral arm of the Milky Way galaxy at 486,000 mph. We are at present 28,000 light years from the centre of the Milky Way. This distance is constantly increasing, because of the expansion of the universe. Eventually, after some billions of years, a great deal of the sky will be dark, when seen through a telescope. But, to the naked eye, it won't look much different, because most of the stars we see now are in the Milky Way, and they will not move away. Local stars will still be visible, because they are gravitationally bound. This means stars in the Milky Way, Andromeda and about 60 nearby, smaller satellite galaxies, including the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds, will still be visible. Of course, this assumes there is some intelligent being to do the seeing.

[Figure: Illustration of the Milky Way spiral galaxy with arms labelled Perseus, Orion-Cygnus, Saggitarius, Norma and Scutum-Crux, and the Sun marked]

headings.text: Expansion of space - impact on what can be seen from Earth

chapters.title: God - The Biggest Question?
chapters.summary: Does He want the whole of humanity, past and present, to know He exists? Try out the answer 'Yes' and then try the answer 'No'. The only answer explained.

pages.text:
Chapter 27

God - The Biggest Question?

Does God want all Modern Humans (MH) to know that He exists?

Some background:

First, bear in mind the typical description of the monotheistic, Christian God. It is claimed He has amazing qualities and abilities. He is fair and kind to everyone, everywhere, i.e. omni-benevolence, omnipresence. Abrahamic faiths believe that God is also transcendent, (outside of space and time) ergo He is not subject to anything arising from what He has created. That's not all, of particularly interest is the claim of God's omniscience and omnipotence. In addition to all this, because of His transcendence, He is eternal. In essence, we have a being who knows everything and is super-supremely powerful and capable, nothing is impossible for Him and he acts justly, wisely and kindly. If this God wants something to happen, it happens, every time, end of story.

Next, who are these 'Modern Humans', referred to in the question above? Well, they are us, and they are all our ancestors, right back to the very beginning of the Homo Sapiens line, some 300,000 years ago. If the answer is "Yes" to the question above, all these MH, every last one of them, has to have undeniable knowledge of a monotheistic God and know clearly what He wants of them. That's some background, now to explore the potential answer "Yes" and the potential answer "No" to this question: 'Does God want all Modern Humans (MH) to know that He exists?'

Try "Yes" as an answer:

This has to be the answer that Christian theologians and Christian church chiefs of every denomination would give. It's impossible for them to answer 'No', after their attempted justification of the Bible, and their promotion of their Christian faith. There are huge problems if attempting to claim the answer is "YES" to the question above. Quite simply, the evidence does not support such a conclusion, by a country mile. Theses issues similarly apply to the two other Abrahamic religions, Islam and Judaism.

99% of the period of time that MH have existed, came before the Abrahamic God made his Biblical appearance. Pre-historic humans, for more than 290,000 years, mostly held beliefs that had nothing to do with a single God. Their beliefs were associated with the natural world and ancestors, some held special reverence for cave bears. None of these beliefs are anything like that

headings.text: Does God want all Modern Humans (MH) to know that He exists?

pages.text:
of the one God promoted by the Bible. The early historic humans, who came after their prehistoric ancestors, had a wide range of deities. From more than 7,000 years ago, civilisation's early front-runners, Sumerians and Egyptians, paid homage to a huge pantheon of anthropomorphic Gods and Goddesses.

Later civilisations did the same. A big shift to just the one God began with the Roman Emperor, Constantine the Great, He started promoting Christianity 1,700 years ago, this was mainly to help unify his Empire. The monotheistic God was not in sight up until him, except for a tiny minority of the world's population.

Even in the shortish time - less than 1% of total human existence - since Abraham and Constantine, many humans have either not known of, or not believed in, the monotheistic God. These are the Buddhists, Hindus, Sikhs, those of many other faiths, and of hundreds of million who have no faith at all. Atheists and agnostics have steadily increased in numbers since the age of enlightenment, 250 years ago.

In conclusion it is abundantly clear that it's incorrect to say that God wants modern humans to know that he exists, because, if he did, he has failed by a very large margin, and God does not do failure we are told. That's a conundrum for monotheistic religions. Therefore, in answer to the question: 'Does God want us, Modern Humans, to know that He exists, "Yes" seems not to be the answer. The clear lack of evidence says so. If not Yes, then the answer must be No, yes? Well, no, as we will see next.

Now try "No" as an answer:

'NO' definitely does not work for Christian faiths. At their very base is the concept of a God who is constantly involved with humans and through sacred texts has given His message. This God is a personal one who can be appealed to and prayed to. These believers cannot say that their God does not want his existence to be known. Of course, there are some deists who might say 'ah yes, God quick-started the universe, then was no longer involved in what happened subsequently. He just stood back and watched from the sidelines, but He's still there all right.' That means he did not want people to know he existed. This horse falls at the very first fence. If a supremely able God did not want modern humans to know he exists, then why do billions think that he does? With his alleged powers He could ensure MH are unaware of his existence, but billions think they know of Him. Clearly, 'No' does not work. It is not the right answer to the question.

The correct and only answer:

Because a God as traditionally described is so unimaginably mighty He can arrange things to his own wishes. Humans cannot out-think, nor outfox Him, this, the claimed creator. It's a puzzle then, since neither a 'Yes' or 'No' answer works. We've reached a point where Conan Doyle's great fictional detective, Sherlock Holmes, would say, "When you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth." In this case what remains is not so improbable - that there is no God. That's the only way to answer the question correctly. The question itself is based on a false premise - that a monotheistic God exists. When that premise is eliminated, God disappears, this seems to be the only reasonable conclusion that can be reached.

[Figure: Diagram: a box reading "Does He want all humans who have ever lived to know for sure that He exists?" above a circle divided into "YES", "NO?" and "Neither one nor the other, and so?" with "G" at the centre]

So, the question does not seem to work because it's based on the assumption of a God, but what do theologians say in answer to it?

Answers given by some theologians:

The question has been asked of some top church believers who were first reminded that modern humans had been around for 300,000 years.

Professor Alister McGrath, Christian theologian, was asked the question at a lecture he gave in Cambridge. He paused before responding, then said, 'That's a very good question.' After pausing again, he said to the questioner "Do you know of Plato's Cave?" The questioner nodded yes, but Alister went on anyway to explain. His point was that we cannot understand God's will and that we have to have 'faith'. The same question, with the same preamble, was asked in a Cambridge debate of Archbishop Rowan Williams. He was under time pressure and clearly thought he did not have much time to give a detailed answer. He replied swiftly, and without any supporting argument said, "Yes". In his book "The Jesus I Never Knew", author Philip Yancey said: "I have learned that faith means trusting in advance what will only make sense in reverse." Yancey said that God gave us the freedom to believe in him or not. Relying again on faith, not on evidence. The question remains unanswered, i.e. what does this God want to happen?

In conclusion:

In these three attempted answers in the preceding paragraph, humans are basically asked to have faith and believe in God because we cannot really know, or understand, what He is up to. This seems not good enough by a long stretch. Why, if there is a God, has He allowed very serious doubts to arise about His existence because of the large number of problematic issues with the Bible, among other difficulties. Added to this, he has failed to give any clear evidence of his existence over the whole of Modern Humans 300,000 year sojourn on planet Earth.

Humans evolved from a series of upright bipeds. At each stage of the bipedal evolution one major change was the increase in brain size. If a God was in charge of this evolutionary process He ensured we, MH had bigger, better brains than our predecessors in the Homo line. In which case surely this means He wants us to be able to clearly work out the origin of everything? If He wants us to have 'freewill' in deciding whether or not to believe in Him it's reasonable to think that He must give more than hints, which are so weak they can be shot down in flames. He must also make things clear to all MH, from our very outset, 300,000 years ago. He has not done this, so the only reasonable assessment is to conclude there is no indisputable evidence of His existence. No "Yes" no "No" then no God.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.summary: 7 possible answers plus 42. The significance of the number 7. Hello, hello, hello = Dixon of Dock Green

pages.text:
Chapter 28

Conclusions

We've seen how the notion of spirits, Gods, or finally the one God, has permeated every sphere and every period of Modern Humans' existence. As explained in earlier chapters, there's compelling reasons for this: the safety deposit box; evolutionary advantage; comfort blanket; clubbiness; promise of eternal life in paradise; the fear of hell, or equivalent; the attempted COTHAM six proofs and PSR - Principle of Sufficient Reason; the cajoling and threats made by clerics or government leaders, and the simple, but so powerful, "acceptance" - belief via location. Added to this is the proven predilection of children towards credence in the supernatural. It's no wonder we've had a myriad of religions and a multitude of Gods and Goddesses, with the Abrahamic God now firmly in the lead

Many philosophers, scientists, theologians, artists, fiction writers as well as "ordinary" people have pondered the issue: is there really a God(s), and if not what else? Despite huge efforts by lots of extremely clever individuals, proof of an omnipotent being's existence remains elusive. There seems to be no clear evidence. Some would say there is no evidence at all, particular having in mind the relentless march of scientific discoveries. The origin of the universe, or universes, is not yet fully known, but is less of a mystery now than in the past. Much of what was thought to be due to "the will of God" by previous generations is now explainable in scientific terms. Darwin's uncovering of evolution put a spanner in Godly creationism. It is increasingly harder for religious leaders to point to the guiding hand of God in forming our universe and shaping man's part in it. Cosmologists and theoretical physicists have been able to offer theories to support the natural development of the universe, from the Big Bang onwards. We now know that both mankind and the planet we live on are tiny parts of an enormous universal whole, and our universe may be just one of countless others. Despite these great strides forward, science, same as religion, has not yet come up with a final, provable answer to the origin of everything.

The deepest sin against the human mind is to believe things without evidence.

Aldous Huxley, author of Brave New World

Those who do think there is a God often do so because they are encouraged to believe in some form of ancient religious texts. These have been written exclusively by men. It's curious that half of Modern Humans - women - were not involved.

The male authors have long since died. They cannot be cross-examined about either the evidence or logic base for their written creeds. What it boils down to is that God has adherents, usually goodly people, who have faith, belief, or simple unquestioning acceptance. They may have one or all of these but they do not have incontrovertible proof. There is not one shred of hard evidence for any type of God. This is despite the efforts made over thousands of years by theologians and various clerics.

Research shows that most philosophers and many scientists do not see any evidence or logic to show there is a God. Paul Dirac and Carl Sagan, among others, are of this view. These are atheists. Some are just doubtful - agnostics.  Philosophers such as Soren Kierkegaard and William James claim that there is a limit to use of reason. They suggest that it is right to employ the leap of faith when that limit is reached. Is this a leap into the light or into the dark?

Some fence sitters are dubious about their religion and doubt God, but hope that He exists. The prospect of eternal bliss, or re-incarnation after Earthly death, is alluring, and the clubbiness engendered from embracing a religion is comforting. For these people, hedging one's bet seems a good idea - just as Blaise Pascal argued. It's reasonable to conjecture that there are many such people. These are the half-hearted supporters of one or other religion.

The materialistic, hard-headed, modern world has probably thrown up a larger corps of non-believers than at any time in recorded history. People may not believe because they are too tied up in the process of living. They have no faith because they do not need it to pursue and enjoy their lives. Other people research the issue and then decide they cannot believe in a religion or God. To change perceptions up front blatant proof is needed that He exists. This simply is not to be found. For those that seriously ponder this issue all that can be done is take one of three approaches, either have blind faith in some type of religion, hold a form of atheistic non-belief or be a 'don't know'. The latter two types are influenced by the lack of evidence. The former, the religious and spiritual people, may ignore the lack of hard evidence and have faith in the teachings of a holy book. They may justify the use of faith, just as have Kierkegaard and James. Religious people believe without supporting proof, but similarly atheists do not have absolute evidence for their dis-belief.

The fact is that no religion, or atheism can claim certainty for what they believe or don't believe. We just don't yet know all the answers, yet.

The 'don't knows' - the agnostics - sit between the religious and the atheists. Agnostics are convinced that at present we cannot be certain sure one way or the other. They might speculate on the possibilities that lead to our universe and Modern Humans.

So, what is it that can be conjectured? What are the possibilities that could explain the existence of the cosmos and us – aside from a Poplawski's hyper black hole? No one knows for sure, despite many religious devotees think they do - God started it and made us. Is a God, of some sort involved? Interestingly, author Karen Armstrong touched on this in her detailed, well researched book "A History of God". Karen mentioned that philosopher A.J. Ayer claimed the idea of God only had meaning if it could be either falsified or verified. She went on: "Similarly a traditional believer in the 'Old Man in the Sky' is not making a meaningless statement when he says: 'I believe in God', since after death we should be able to find out whether or not this is true." Here Karen seems to think we will know whether or not God exists, after we die. However, that assumes we will have some sort of conscious afterlife - a very big assumption, completely unproven. If, as the ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus says, death is the end of all sensation, then after death we won't exist and will be incapable of having a clue about anything.

At the moment we can only guess at original cause, death won't tell us the answer, probably. What are the possibilities in the frame to explain the origin of our universe? Here's seven possible answers:

Scientific Rationalism: There is no God. The universe and everything in it, including modern humans, has a scientific explanation, based on eternal mathematics, if only we can find it. The Great Theory of Everything needs to be cracked for this to be proved;
Computer Game: Our whole universe, including us, Modern Humans, operate within a computer programme. We are but bits and bytes, 0 and 1, a little like the film Tron. Everything is based on numbers. Pythagoras, Max Tegmark and Roger Penrose might feel vindicated. We have no reality; our world is virtual and so are we. Super intelligent beings from somewhere in the multiverse are the programmers.

    Imagine another universe 10 billion years older than ours. It's had time for a race of super-beings to evolve. These beings live for 500,000 years. A couple of bright children, just 50,00 and 55,000 years old, have a school exam project. They must design a new universe, using computer binary code.

Of the seven possibilities above, two of them involve a being or beings that we would consider to be a "standard" God, i.e. numbers 4 and 5. Of the rest, four others involve beings with Godlike powers. Only one, number 1, proposes that there is no God, of any variety, concerned with the universe's existence, but one may very well win over the six. None of the answers suggest how the very first of anything came into being. They're all about the possible origin of our universe, or us. But eventually something has to begin from nothing. You cannot have "nothing" according to Parmenides and Rene Descartes, but Berkeley thinks it's all in the mind and Winnie the Pooh finds "nothing" easy.

And from the seven possibilities above the answer is....... I don't know. Do you? Douglas Adams, in his book 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy' attempts to come up with the 'Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, The Universe, and Everything'. Hyper-intelligent mice used the greatest of computers, Deep Thought, to solve this ultimate question. After 7½ million years of convoluted computation Deep Thought finally came up with an answer, 42. At the present stage of human knowledge, 42 is as good a solution as any other.

Deep Thought's answer of 42, does not tell us what came before 42. The super-duper computer does not say how anything, anywhere first came into being, just as the other seven possibles do not. How did a God, a singularity, or anything at all, first come into being? If you know the answer to this one, and can offer proof, you are unique and will have a great TV and media career explaining to everyone.

If you put the question another way though, the answer may be worked out very exactly. Here's the revamped question: "I am the beginning of everything, the end of time and space, the beginning of every end, the end of every place. What am I?" Can you answer? It's really easy at first.

Significance of seven

The total of 7 possibilities - does this number have any significance? Well, for quite a few people it does. God, apparently, took it easy on day 7, after 6 days of hard word setting up Earth, Adam and much else.  A week consists of 7 days. Deep Thought's answer, 42, = 6x7. The Jewish Menorah most often has 7 candles. Snow White had a romp with seven dwarfs. T. E. Lawrence's autobiography was 'The Seven Pillars of Wisdom', not six or eight.

Then there's that traditional English nursery rhyme:

As I was going to St. Ives,
I met a man with seven wives,
Each wife had seven sacks,
Each sack had seven cats,
Each cat had seven kits:
Kits, cats, sacks, and wives,
How many were there going to St. Ives?

None is the answer. The wives got fed up when they reached Newquay, where they met some jolly sailors. Cats, kits, husband and drawers were let loose.

An English phrase indicating extreme bliss is 'seventh heaven'. Seven is the highest Jannah, or heaven, in Islam and there are seven hells. Hinduism gives us the seven great gurus (Rishis). That ancient ascetic monk, Evagrius, came up with the seven deadly sins. St Ambrose and others countered with the seven heavenly virtues. These were formed by the symbolic addition of the 3 theological virtues (faith, hope and charity) with the 4 cardinal ones (prudence, justice, temperance and fortitude). The 7 sins and 7 virtues are a form of dualism, with some similarity to the far-eastern idea of Yin and Yang.

[Figure: Yin and Yang symbol, labelled Yang (light) and Yin (dark)]

In Chinese culture 7 represents the combination of the opposite forces of Yin and Yang (concept of interconnected dualism) together with the 5 elements (Water, Fire, Wood, Metal and Earth). Confucianism views this mixture as representative of harmony. Chinese Taoism sees it as connected with kindness and beauty.

All very interesting, but with the 7 possibilities for our universe, are they just by coincidence, 7, or maybe by convenience and coincidence?

And finally, that book title, Hello, hello, hello

[Figure: Jack Warner was policeman Dixon]

Dixon of Dock Green was a popular BBC TV soap. It ran for more than 429 episodes from 1955 to 1976. In the days of Dixon, bobbies (policemen) pounded the beat, i.e. they walked the streets of their patch. Dixon, a bobby, was a vital community character, gently putting right all the wrongs in his neighbourhood.

In a parallel universe Dixon was a real figure, this time he came from the west country of England, rather than London. On one occasion, while plodding his Bristol beat, he saw a discarded copy of "Hello", a celebrity news magazine. "Ello, 'ello, 'ello" said Dixon, as he bent down to pick it up - h's were an anathema to him - "what have we 'ear." His spelling wasn't too hot either.

Little did he know, but the dark dot in the top right corner of the magazine was a super-microdot. It contained a detailed message from God explaining how He had kick-started the universe. Also answered by the dot were man's many questions about why we are here, what's it all about, and who will win the World Cup.

[Figure: Earth beside a panel reading "Why? What? How? Who?"]

Gabriel had tried to persuade God to use social media rather than "Hello" to give his explanatory message to mankind, but God said: "Well, it's a magazine telling stories about celebrities and I'm the greatest story and the greatest celebrity ever. The super-microdot will let me fit everything in, otherwise the magazine would run to 25,000 pages, then poor Dixon wouldn't be able to pick it up. Some clever-clogs is bound to notice the dot and will tell all the other humans."

You can keep a look out for that magazine, but I fear you won't find it. We are in the wrong universe. Hello and goodbye.

Chart titled "Standard Model of Elementary Particles", with the headings "12 Matter Particles (Fermions)" and "4 Force carrying Particles + Higgs". Each particle is shown as a coloured circle in a box, with its mass, charge and spin (key at left: mass, charge, spin). Quarks (purple): up (u) 2/3, 1/2; charm (c) 2/3, 1/2; top (t) 2/3, 1/2; down (d) ≈4.8 MeV/c², -1/3, 1/2; strange (s) ≈95 MeV/c², -1/3, 1/2; bottom (b) ≈4.18 GeV/c², -1/3, 1/2. Leptons (green): electron (e) ≈0.511 MeV/c², -1, 1/2; muon (μ) ≈105.67 MeV/c², -1, 1/2; tau (τ) ≈1.7768 GeV/c², -1, 1/2; electron neutrino (νe) <2.2 eV/c², 0, 1/2; muon neutrino (νμ) <1.7 MeV/c², 0, 1/2; tau neutrino (ντ) <15.5 MeV/c², 0, 1/2. Gauge bosons (red): gluon (g) 0, 1; photon (γ) 0, 0, 1; Z boson (Z) ≈91.19 GeV/c², 0, 1; W boson (W) ≈80.39 GeV/c², ±1, 1. Scalar bosons (yellow): Higgs (H) 0, 0
